# Assumptions, uncertainty & scope

What this agent assumes, what it can't know, and what it deliberately doesn't do.
The agent repeats the relevant parts in its answers (the `assumptions` and `limitations` fields).

## What the score means and doesn't mean
- **It measures exposure, not loss.** It shows how often hazardous weather hits a hub's location. It does
  **not** include hub volume or revenue, building quality, existing resilience upgrades, insurance,
  or how well the local area copes. "Most exposed" ≠ "most expensive".
- **Local adaptation is not modeled.** The same 5 cm of snow paralyzes Atlanta but not Minneapolis.
  We use one national threshold per hazard (an absolute scale). Southern cold and ice exposure is partly covered by
  FEMA's ice storm and cold wave frequencies. *Later:* per-hub local thresholds.
- **All hubs are treated as equally important.** We have no shipment or revenue data. *Later:* optional volume weighting.
- Scores are **decision support**. Final investment decisions belong to the team.

## Location
- A hub = the metro's **city-center point**. Real warehouses often sit near the airport or on the metro's edge,
  possibly in a different county.
- Weather is read for that point from a ~9–11 km model grid. FEMA data is for the **county** that contains the point.

## Data sources & their limits
| Source | Used for | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) | Daily snowfall, min temperature, precipitation, max wind gust, max apparent temperature, 2021-01-01 → yesterday, in each hub's local calendar day | It's **modeled reanalysis, not station measurements**: it smooths peaks, so wind gusts in particular are underestimated. The last few days are **preliminary** and get revised, so we re-fetch the last 7 every night. The free tier is **non-commercial**: a real deployment needs a paid plan. Data is licensed CC-BY 4.0 (attribution shown in the UI). |
| [FEMA National Risk Index v1.20 (Dec 2025)](https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/data-resources) via its public [ArcGIS county service](https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Counties/FeatureServer/0) | Annualized frequency of hurricane, tornado, hail, inland and coastal flooding, ice storm, winter weather, cold wave, heat wave, strong wind | County-level. Built from long historical records, so it **changes slowly** and won't reflect last year's events. Riverine flood is now called `IFLD` (Inland Flooding). |

## Time window
- Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest available day, so they move slightly every night.
- "Last year" means **calendar 2025** unless the user says otherwise. The agent states the period it used.
- 5 years is short for rare events (hurricanes, big ice storms). That's why those rely on FEMA's long-record frequencies.

## Thresholds (checked against US National Weather Service criteria)
NWS sets most warning criteria **per local office**, so there is rarely one national number. We picked one
national value per hazard, close to typical NWS warning levels:

| Day type | Our threshold | NWS reference | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snow day | ≥ 1 cm snowfall | No NWS daily definition | A reasonable "measurable snow" proxy |
| Heavy snow day | ≥ 15 cm (~6 in) | Winter Storm Warning: locally set, roughly 4–12 in ([NWSI 10-513](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005013curr.pdf), [criteria map](https://www.weather.gov/snow-criteria)). Denver: 6 in/12 h ([BOU](https://www.weather.gov/bou/winterguide)) | Southern offices use lower values |
| Extreme cold day | min temp ≤ −18 °C (0 °F) | Extreme Cold Warning (replaced Wind Chill Warning on 2024-10-01, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/243009-cold-hazard-simplification)). Locally set, from about 0 °F (South) to −35 °F (North) | Uses air temperature, not wind chill |
| Heavy rain day | ≥ 50 mm (~2 in) | **No NWS daily rain threshold**: flood warnings are impact-based. NOAA tracks heavy days as the top 1% locally ([USGCRP](https://www.globalchange.gov/indicators/heavy-precipitation)) | Arid hubs rarely reach 50 mm. Their flash-flood exposure comes through FEMA |
| High wind day | gust ≥ 93 km/h (58 mph) | High Wind Warning: sustained ≥ 40 mph or gusts ≥ 58 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)) | Exact match |
| Wind advisory day | gust ≥ 72 km/h (45 mph) | Wind Advisory: sustained 30–39 mph (NWSI 10-515). The 45 mph gust value is our own choice | **The wind signal we actually score on.** The Step 2 check over 5 years: warning-level days were 0–1/yr (13 of 36 hubs at 0, because modeled data smooths peaks, though single storms do show up, e.g. Tampa 153 km/h during Hurricane Milton), while advisory days were 0.2–8.6/yr |
| Extreme heat day | apparent temp max ≥ 40 °C (~105 °F) | Extreme Heat Warning (renamed from Excessive Heat Warning 2025-03-04, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/250310-heat-hazard)): heat index ~105–110 °F, locally set | Open-Meteo's "apparent temperature" is a different formula from the NWS heat index |

## Out of scope (Phase 1)
- **Dust storms.** FEMA has no dust hazard. NOAA's [Storm Events Database](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/)
  has "Dust Storm" events by forecast zone (84 nationwide in 2023, mostly TX/AZ/CA). Dust storm warning criteria:
  visibility ≤ ¼ mile with winds usually ≥ 25 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)).
  Planned as the first post-deploy feature.
- Wildfire smoke, earthquakes, lightning and drought (FEMA has some of these, but they aren't weather-disruption
  hazards in our brief).
- Forecasts and live alerts. Phase 1 is historical exposure only.
- Cities that aren't in our hub list. The agent says so instead of guessing.

## Operational limits of the demo deployment
- The OpenRouter key has a **$20 credit cap** and **expires 7 days after creation (around 2026-12-02)**.
  After that the agent can't answer until a new key is set in Vercel's environment variables.
- Open-Meteo's free tier is per-IP and non-commercial. A production version needs their paid API.

## Uncertainty the agent communicates
- **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed in code from data completeness (≥95% of days present) and
  the number of sources backing each hazard (observed + FEMA).
- Every answer lists the assumptions and limitations that apply to it.

# 🦉 The Daily Prophet — Plan

Agreed on 2026-11-25 after a structured "grilling" session (see `docs/session/`).
Every individual choice and its reason is in [decisions.md](decisions.md).

## Goal
A chat agent that helps logistics analysts decide which distribution hubs are most
exposed to severe weather and should get resilience investment. It ranks, compares
and explains hubs using **deterministic, tested scoring code**. The LLM only chooses
tools and explains their results. It never invents numbers.

## Architecture (target)
```
Browser (Next.js UI: Roboto, dark glass)
  │  POST /api/chat {sessionId, message}  → streams progress + text + validated answer
  │  GET  /api/widgets                    → top hubs, hazard leaders, data status
  ▼
proxy.ts — Basic Auth on everything except /api/cron/* (uses CRON_SECRET)
  ▼
src/app/api/*  (thin: Zod-parse → call core → format response/errors)
  ▼
src/core/  (no Next.js; testable alone)
  agent/   AI SDK v7 streamText + 4 tools + Output.object(answer schema)
           → validate → code overrides confidence/disclaimer → retry once → error
  tools/   rank_hubs · compare_hubs · get_weather_stat · explain_hub_score
  scoring/ pure: thresholds → per-hazard 0–100 → overall → level → confidence
  stats/   pure: counts / % / ranges over daily rows
  ingest/  incremental: Open-Meteo + FEMA → DB → scoring → nightly snapshot
  db/      Supabase repositories (server-only secret key)
  ▼                    ▼                          ▼
Supabase Postgres   OpenRouter (LLM + Jev)   Open-Meteo archive · FEMA NRI ArcGIS
        ▲
Vercel Cron (daily) → /api/cron/ingest      npm run ingest (first full load, local)
```

## Database tables
Every table has `created_at` + `updated_at` (trigger-maintained). RLS on, no public policies.

| Table | Holds |
|---|---|
| `hubs` | id slug, name, state, Census region, lat/lon, timezone, county FIPS/name, active |
| `weather_daily` | hub × date: snowfall, min temp, precipitation, max gust, max apparent temp |
| `fema_nri` | per hub: NRI version + annualized frequency per hazard + raw record |
| `score_snapshots` | per hub per ingest run: overall, level, top hazard, breakdown, confidence, window, scoring_version |
| `chat_sessions`, `chat_messages` | server-side conversation memory incl. tool results |
| `events` | append-only log (ingest, scoring, validation failures, retries, guard decisions, errors), grouped by `correlation_id` |

## Scoring (summary)
- 6 hazards and weights: hurricane 25%, winter 20%, flood/rain 20%, severe storms (tornado + hail) 15%, wind 10%, heat 10%.
- Each hazard is scored 0–100 on a fixed absolute scale. Mixed hazards are 50% observed (Open-Meteo) + 50% FEMA annualized frequency.
- Overall = 60% weighted average + 40% highest hazard. Levels: Low 0–33, Medium 34–66, High 67–100.
- Confidence (High/Medium/Low) is computed in code from data completeness and the number of sources.
- Rolling 5-year window ending at the newest available day. The relative rank among hubs is shown next to the score.

## Steps (one branch + PR each; Yarden merges)
| # | Step | New env vars |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Supabase project, scaffold, lint boundary, Vitest, env validation, error helper, schema + events, 36-hub seed, docs, session export | `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY` |
| 2 | Open-Meteo + FEMA clients, incremental paced ingest, first full load, check wind-gust distribution | — |
| 3 | Anchor values reviewed with real data → scoring test-first → snapshots | — |
| 4 | Agent: tools, answer schema + validation + retry, recommendation rules, chat history | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_MODEL` |
| 5 | Streaming `POST /api/chat`, `/api/widgets`, cron route, Basic Auth | `APP_USERNAME`, `APP_PASSWORD`, `CRON_SECRET` |
| 6 | UI: chat, 3 widgets, per-answer charts | — |
| 7 | Eval set (13 cases) + `npm run eval` (`--url` for deployed) | — |
| 8 | Model bakeoff (3–4 models: accuracy → cost → speed), lock in the winner | — |
| 9 | README, design doc, final assumptions | — |
| 10 | Deploy to Vercel, env vars, cron, run evals against live URL | (same, in Vercel) |
| 11 | Phase 1.5: Jev guard (`typesafe/jev-1.14`, cutoff 0.4, 2 s fail-open, last 2 turns) + guard evals + cutoff tuning | `JEV_MODEL` |

## Later (order to be chosen)
Themed login page · dust storm hazard (NOAA Storm Events) · US map widget · abuse/off-topic
hardening · score-change alerts · 7-day forecast + NWS active alerts · per-hub local
thresholds · hub volume weighting · voice.

4. "Why is Dallas high?" premise check. 5. False premise (Seattle hurricane). 6. Follow-up "why that one?".
7. Overall top 5. 8. Unknown city (Boise). 9. Dust storm (not scored). 10. Decision question.
11. Off-topic. 12. "Last year" = 2025. 13. Confidence matches code.

# 🦉 The Daily Prophet

A weather risk intelligence agent for a logistics company's US distribution hubs.
Analysts chat with it to find out which hubs are most exposed to severe weather, compare hubs,
and understand *why* a hub is risky, to help decide where to invest in resilience upgrades.

> 🚧 Work in progress. Built step by step. See [docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md).

## Docs
- [Plan](docs/plan.md): architecture, tables, steps
- [Decision log](docs/decisions.md): every choice and why
- [Assumptions, uncertainty & scope](docs/assumptions.md)
- [Design](docs/design.md)
- [AI session log](docs/session/): the full conversation with the coding agent

## Run locally
Requirements: Node 22+, a Supabase project.

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local     # then fill in the values (see comments in the file)
npm run db:check               # verifies the database connection: lists the hubs
npm run dev                    # http://localhost:3000
```

## Scripts
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` | Start the app locally |
| `npm test` | Unit tests (Vitest) |
| `npm run typecheck` | TypeScript check |
| `npm run lint` | ESLint (includes the rule keeping `src/core` free of Next.js) |
| `npm run db:check` | Connect to Supabase and list hubs per region |
| `npm run ingest` | Fetch FEMA + Open-Meteo data for all active hubs (incremental; the first full load takes about 1 h because of Open-Meteo's rate limits) |
| `npm run ingest -- --hub=dallas,denver` | Same, for selected hubs only |
| `npm run session:export -- <file.jsonl>` | Export the AI session log to `docs/session/` (scrubbed) |

## Database
SQL migrations live in [supabase/migrations/](supabase/migrations/). Apply them in order to a fresh
Supabase project (SQL editor or Supabase CLI). The second migration seeds the 36 hubs.

## Data attribution
Weather data by [Open-Meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com/) (CC BY 4.0). Hazard data: FEMA National Risk Index.

@AGENTS.md

# The Daily Prophet: project rules

A weather-risk agent for logistics hubs (take-home assignment). Read before any work:
[docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md) for architecture and the step list, [docs/decisions.md](docs/decisions.md)
for every agreed choice and its reason, and [docs/assumptions.md](docs/assumptions.md) for data limits.

## Teamwork: decide together
Yarden and Claude are one team. Decisions are made together, not by Claude alone.
- **Ask first** about anything that changes product behavior, data or its meaning, architecture,
  dependencies, DB schema, scoring, or what users see. Give a recommendation, then wait.
- **Do and log** the mechanical things: naming inside a function, test structure, formatting, type fixes.
- **Unsure which?** Ask.
- Every agreed decision goes into `docs/decisions.md` in plain language ("What / Why").
  Assumptions and data limits go into `docs/assumptions.md`.

## Workflow
- Small steps. One branch and one PR per step. Yarden reviews and merges. Claude never merges or pushes to `main`.
- After each step: say what was done and what's next, then wait for an OK.
- Before each step: list the `.env` variables it will need.
- PR bodies explain the decisions made and the evidence (test output, data checks).
- Refresh the session log with `npm run session:export`. Its built-in leak check must pass before the log is committed.

## Before writing code
1. **Reuse.** Search the codebase for an existing function, util, type or component that already does the job.
2. **Usages.** Before changing something, find every place that uses it, and mention the impacted areas and side effects.
3. **Single source of truth.** Each fact lives in one place. Derive what can be derived. If you see the same
   state, config or schema in two places, flag it before coding. When a copy is unavoidable (e.g. a DB
   constraint mirrored in a TS type), a test must fail when they drift.
4. **Fewest moving parts.** Between plans with the same outcome, pick the one with fewer things that can fail
   (network calls, manual steps, multi-step migrations, parallel writes).

## Code rules
- **`src/core/` stays framework-free:** no Next.js or React imports (enforced by ESLint).
- **JSDoc** on every exported and internal function, class, method and type. Explain clearly and simply.
- **Errors.** Wrap every boundary operation (external API, DB, LLM, Jev, API route, script entry point) in
  try/catch and rethrow as `BoundaryError` (`src/core/errors/boundaryError.ts`), which formats
  `ErrorName || message || functionName || emoji` with a fixed emoji per boundary. Pure functions (scoring,
  stats, parsing) throw plain errors and leave formatting to the boundary. When you deliberately continue
  after an error, log it in the same format.
- **Timeouts on every external call, no exceptions.** HTTP: `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` (or an
  `AbortController`). Supabase: the client's wrapped `fetch`. LLM calls: the AI SDK timeout/abort option.
- **Secrets** live only in `.env.local` (local) and Vercel env vars (prod). `.env.example` lists every variable.
- **After every migration:** regenerate `src/core/db/database.types.ts` from the live schema.
- **The LLM never produces numbers.** Scores and stats come from tested TypeScript, and the LLM picks tools and explains.

## Honesty
- **Verify before claiming.** Before saying a file, function, table, column, env var, package, endpoint,
  command or flag exists, check it: read the file, grep the symbol, query the schema, run `--help`.
  When unsure, say so explicitly.
- **Honesty over precision** for end users too: when our data measures something poorly, the agent says so
  plainly instead of presenting a weak number as fact.
- Be candid with Yarden: criticize plans and code, including your own, when something is wrong.

## Vibes
Love cats 🐱. Use cat emojis in chat and UI copy where they fit 😸. Error-boundary emojis stay as defined in
`boundaryError.ts`.

## Hard-won lessons
Each one: *next time you see X → do Y*.
1. **`npm run x -- --flag` on PowerShell** → the `--` is swallowed and the flag arrives as env var
   `npm_config_flag`. Read both `process.argv` and `process.env.npm_config_*`.
2. **"This API probably lags N days / returns shape X"** → probe the real API first. Open-Meteo's archive
   served data up to yesterday, not 5 days back as assumed.
3. **Supabase pause fails with "hibernating"** → it can't be paused through the API. Ask Yarden to pause it in
   the dashboard.
4. **A long Bash heredoc fails with "unexpected EOF"** → write files with the Write tool.
5. **Weather data shows (near) zero extreme events** → check whether reanalysis smoothing is hiding the peaks
   before concluding "safe". Gusts ≥93 km/h were 0–1/yr even in windy hubs, so we score on ≥72 km/h.
6. **"Untracked working tree files would be overwritten" after switching to an older `main`** → compare file
   hashes against the target commit before any reset. The files were identical and nothing was lost.

## Summary

Step 3 of [the plan](docs/plan.md): **the deterministic scoring engine.** Every hub gets a 0–100 score per hazard, an overall score, a Low/Medium/High level, a top hazard and a confidence label, all from tested TypeScript with no LLM involved. Every number comes from **one file**, [`src/core/scoring/config.ts`](src/core/scoring/config.ts). The anchors and combination rules were decided together (S1–S11) from the real data spread and a national comparison across 3,232 US counties.

```text
npm run ingest                      (or: npm run score — re-score only, no API calls)
  runIngestThenScore                # src/core/pipeline — one run id for fetch + score
    runIngest                       # Step 2, unchanged (+ --refresh-fema)
    runScoring                      # src/core/scoring/runScoring.ts (I/O injected)
      for each active hub
        scoringWindow(latest)       # last 1,826 days
        getWeatherDays (paged)      # PostgREST caps responses at 1,000 rows → .range() pages
        computeObservedSignals      # pure: hazard days per year + coverage
        scoreHub                    # pure:
          computeHazardScores       #   6 hazards × (observed half, FEMA half) → 0–100
            linearScore             #   0 → 0, anchor → 100, capped
            hybridConfidence        #   complete data + LIKE-FOR-LIKE source agreement
          computeOverall            #   60% weighted avg + 40% worst hazard
          riskLevelFor              #   Low 0–33 · Medium 34–66 · High 67–100
      saveScoreSnapshots            # ONE insert for all hubs
```

### How each hazard is built

| Hazard (weight) | Observed half | FEMA half (100 = national p95) | Cross-check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hurricane (25%) | none | hurricane | none: FEMA only, 170-yr record |
| Winter (20%) | **max**(snow days, extreme-cold days) | **max**(winter weather, cold wave, ice storm) | snow/cold vs winter weather/cold wave (ice excluded, observed can't see it) |
| Flood (20%) | heavy-rain days | **max**(inland, coastal) | **none**: rain ≠ flood warnings |
| Severe storms (15%) | none | **avg**(tornado **per 1,000 sq mi**, hail) | none: FEMA only |
| Wind (10%) | gust ≥72 km/h days | strong wind | direct |
| Heat (10%) | feels-like ≥40 °C days | heat wave | direct |

## Decisions (D47–D58)

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D47 | FEMA 100 = **national 95th-percentile county** | National yardstick. With p99, no hub reached High (even Miami was 65.8) |
| D48 | Observed 100 = round "severe" levels (snow 40, cold 30, rain 5, gusts 10, heat 60 days/yr) | There's no national dataset. Easy to say out loud |
| D49 | **Max** for distinct events, **average** for tornado + hail | Averaging made Minneapolis's winter only 65. Max for storms put 9 hubs at 100 |
| D50 | Heavy-snow days are reported, not scored | 23 of 36 hubs at 0, so modeled data can't separate hubs |
| D51 | Confidence = complete data + sources agree. Hub = weakest hazard | "One source = Medium" would have made hurricane permanently Medium |
| D52 | Mountain counties (Seattle, SLC) are flagged by D51, not hand-corrected | Honest and automatic |
| D53 | **Tornado per county area** + `county_area_sq_mi` column + `--refresh-fema` | FEMA spreads tornado frequency by area (rank r = +0.62). Phoenix scored 66 raw vs **6** per area |
| D54 | Score at the end of every ingest (same run id). Rank derived at read time | One source of truth |
| D55 | Window = last 1,826 days. Rate = count × 365.25 ÷ days with data | Missing days don't drag rates down |
| D56 | **Cross-check compares like with like** | The first live run had **32 of 36** hubs Medium (flood and ice were structural differences, not data problems). Now **15 of 36**, each with a nameable reason |
| D57 | ⚠️ FEMA flood half caps out for 15 hubs. **Kept, and revisit in Step 7** | The observed half still separates them |
| D58 | Trial snapshots deleted (approved), kept **v1**, deletion logged as an event | Clean history plus an audit trail |

## Evidence

**Tests:** `Test Files 22 passed · Tests 106 passed`. Type check, lint and build are clean. The scoring tests were **written first and seen failing**:
```text
 FAIL  src/core/scoring/*.test.ts (6 files)     ← before implementation
 Test Files 22 passed · Tests 106 passed        ← after
```
They use hand-calculated cases, e.g. Minneapolis winter = (max(52, 86.7) + max(66.1, 86.3, 31.3)) / 2 = **86.5**, and "a tornado count in a 4× bigger county scores 4× lower". The S9 fix was also test-first: 4 red tests went green.

**Two bugs caught on the way:**
- `reason` vs `confidenceReason`: every test passed, but `tsc` caught it. Now covered by a test, and lesson #7 in `CLAUDE.md`.
- Without paging, PostgREST would have returned only 1,000 of 1,826 days. Lesson #8.

**Live run** (`npm run ingest` → fetch + score, run `78b5b203…`): 36 scored, 0 failed. Ingest and scoring events share one run id.

| Level | Hubs |
|---|---|
| **High (8)** | New Orleans 73.9 · Tampa 72.9 · Dallas 72.4 · Jacksonville 70.0 · Oklahoma City 69.6 · Miami 69.3 · Orlando 69.3 · Houston 69.1 |
| **Medium (26)** | e.g. Boston 60.3 (hurricane) · Minneapolis 59.9 (winter) · Denver 57.9 (severe storms) · Phoenix 54.5 (heat) · Seattle 37.3 (winter) |
| **Low (2)** | Albuquerque 28.7 · San Francisco 20.5 |

**Confidence after D56:** 21 High, 15 Medium (wind 10, heat 8, winter 1 = **Seattle**, the mountain-county case it was meant to catch).

**National anchors** (`npm run fema:anchors`, NRI Dec 2025, 3,232 counties): hurricane 0.248 · tornado 0.987 per 1,000 sq mi · hail 8.169 · inland flood 3.536 · coastal flood 4.917 · ice storm 1.548 · winter weather 25.079 · cold wave 10.368 · heat wave 17.842 · strong wind 6.191.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

The migration only adds a nullable column. Snapshots are append-only. The deleted trial rows were approved (S11) and logged.

**Blast Radius:** small

New modules. `scripts/ingest.ts` now also scores (about 30 s more).

## Env vars

None new.

## Next: Step 4 (the agent)

Before writing code, I'll bring you a short round on:
- the system prompt's honesty rules
- the exact tool inputs and outputs, including rank derived at read time
- how the limitations above reach answers
- the first model to start with

Step 4 needs `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, already in `.env.local`, and `OPENROUTER_MODEL`, which we'll pick together.

Step 3 of [the plan](docs/plan.md): **the deterministic scoring engine.** Every hub gets a 0–100 score per hazard, an overall score, a Low/Medium/High level, a top hazard and a confidence label, all from tested TypeScript with no LLM involved. Every number comes from **one file**, [`src/core/scoring/config.ts`](src/core/scoring/config.ts). The anchors and combination rules were decided together (S1–S11) from the real data spread and a national comparison across 3,232 US counties.

```text
npm run ingest                      (or: npm run score — re-score only, no API calls)
  runIngestThenScore                # src/core/pipeline — one run id for fetch + score
    runIngest                       # Step 2, unchanged (+ --refresh-fema)
    runScoring                      # src/core/scoring/runScoring.ts (I/O injected)
      for each active hub
        scoringWindow(latest)       # last 1,826 days
        getWeatherDays (paged)      # PostgREST caps responses at 1,000 rows → .range() pages
        computeObservedSignals      # pure: hazard days per year + coverage
        scoreHub                    # pure:
          computeHazardScores       #   6 hazards × (observed half, FEMA half) → 0–100
            linearScore             #   0 → 0, anchor → 100, capped
            hybridConfidence        #   complete data + LIKE-FOR-LIKE source agreement
          computeOverall            #   60% weighted avg + 40% worst hazard
          riskLevelFor              #   Low 0–33 · Medium 34–66 · High 67–100
      saveScoreSnapshots            # ONE insert for all hubs
```

| Hazard (weight) | Observed half | FEMA half (100 = national p95) | Cross-check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hurricane (25%) | none | hurricane | none: FEMA only, 170-yr record |
| Winter (20%) | **max**(snow days, extreme-cold days) | **max**(winter weather, cold wave, ice storm) | snow/cold vs winter weather/cold wave (ice excluded, observed can't see it) |
| Flood (20%) | heavy-rain days | **max**(inland, coastal) | **none**: rain ≠ flood warnings |
| Severe storms (15%) | none | **avg**(tornado **per 1,000 sq mi**, hail) | none: FEMA only |
| Wind (10%) | gust ≥72 km/h days | strong wind | direct |
| Heat (10%) | feels-like ≥40 °C days | heat wave | direct |

| D50 | Heavy-snow days are reported, not scored | 23 of 36 hubs at 0, so modeled data can't separate hubs |
| D51 | Confidence = complete data + sources agree. Hub = weakest hazard | "One source = Medium" would have made hurricane permanently Medium |

content.text:
**[PR #4](https://github.com/yardenfarag/Home-Assignment-Moveo/pull/4): the scoring engine is ready for review.** All 36 hubs are scored from live data with no failures. 😸

**What's in it:**
- **One file holds every number**, [`scoring/config.ts`](src/core/scoring/config.ts): thresholds, anchors, weights, risk levels and confidence rules.
- **Scoring code that's deterministic and was written test-first.** 106 tests pass, including hand-calculated cases like Minneapolis's winter score of 86.5.
- **Tornado risk is now measured per county area**, which needed a new database column and an `--refresh-fema` option. Phoenix's tornado score dropped from 66 to 6.
- **The ingest now scores automatically when it finishes**, under the same run ID. `npm run score` re-scores without calling any APIs.

**Results:**
- **High (8):** New Orleans 73.9, Tampa 72.9, Dallas 72.4, Jacksonville 70.0, Oklahoma City 69.6, Miami 69.3, Orlando 69.3, Houston 69.1.
- **Low (2):** Albuquerque 28.7, San Francisco 20.5.
- **Medium:** the other 26.
- **Confidence:** 21 hubs High, 15 Medium. I re-checked those numbers against the database just now. Of the 15, 10 are flagged for wind, 8 for heat (some hubs for both) and 1 for winter. The winter one is Seattle, exactly the mountain-county case it was meant to catch.

**Three things I caught myself, all fixed and documented:**
1. **The confidence label was nearly meaningless at first:** 32 of 36 hubs came out Medium. The fix was decided together (S9) and brought it to 15.
2. **A bug that passed every test.** The explanation text for confidence was stored under the wrong field name. The type checker caught it, and there's now a test for it.
3. **A silent data cut-off.** Supabase returns at most 1,000 rows per request, but scoring needs about 1,826 days per hub. Without paging, every hub would have been scored on roughly half its data.

The two code traps (2 and 3), plus the confidence lesson, are now hard-won lessons 7–9 in `CLAUDE.md`. The flood cap you asked to keep an eye on (S10) is recorded in the decision log, the limitations doc and the plan's Step 7 line.

**Next is Step 4, the agent.** Once you've merged, I'll start with a short question round before writing any code:
- the honesty rules in the agent's instructions
- exactly what each tool takes and returns
- how the limitations reach users in answers
- which model to start with

`OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is already in `.env.local`, and we'll pick `OPENROUTER_MODEL` together.

content.text:
Confirmed in the SDK's own docs and types: `streamText` and `generateText` accept **tools and `Output.object` together** (`stopWhen: isStepCount(n)`), and there's a fine-grained `timeout` setting (`totalMs`, `stepMs`, `toolMs`). Here's the Step 4 round.

## Step 4: the agent, question round

❓ **G1** - **The 4 tools: inputs and outputs.** All numbers come from stored snapshots or the weather table, never from the model:

| Tool | Input | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `rank_hubs` | `region?`, `hazard?` (or overall), `limit` 1–36 (default 5), `order` most/least | hubs with score, level, **rank among all 36** (computed when read), top hazard, confidence |
| `compare_hubs` | `hubIds` (2–5), `hazards?` | per hub: overall, level, rank, and per-hazard score (observed and FEMA halves, confidence and reason) |
| `get_weather_stat` | `hubId`, `metric` (fixed list), period: `year`, a date range, or `last12Months`, optional `month` | count, days with data, % of days, threshold used, coverage, caveat |
| `explain_hub_score` | `hubId` | full breakdown: every input (value, unit, the value that maps to 100, score), weights, the formula with its actual numbers, level, rank, confidence reasons |

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G2** - **Units: US first, metric in brackets, converted by code.** Your analysts are American, so "6 in (15 cm)" and "105 °F (40 °C)". Tools return **both** units. If the model converted units itself, it would be inventing numbers.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G3** - **How we enforce "the LLM never invents numbers":**
- **Strict:** every entry in `dataUsed` must match a value a tool actually returned (allowing for rounding). If one doesn't match, the answer fails validation, we retry once, and then return a clear error.
- **Soft:** numbers in the free-text answer that don't appear in any tool result are **logged as a warning event and flagged by the evals**, but not blocked. Text has years, "5-year window" and so on, so a hard block would misfire.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G4** - **Caveats are guaranteed by code.** Each hazard and stat has standing caveats, kept in one file, `scoring/caveats.ts`. Examples: "heavy rain ≠ flooding", "warning-level gusts are undercounted by modeled data", "Seattle's FEMA county includes mountains". Tools attach them, and **code makes sure** the answer's `limitations` includes the caveats for every hazard or metric used. The model can add caveats, but it can't drop ours. This is honesty over precision, enforced.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G5** - **Checking the question's premise, decided by code.** The model only extracts the claim from the question, e.g. `{ hubId: "dallas", claimedLevel: "high", hazard?: … }`. **Code** looks up the real level and sets `holds: true/false`. So "Why is Seattle's hurricane risk high?" is corrected by code, not by the model's judgment.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G6** - **Confidence for each answer type, set by code:**
- **Score answers:** the weakest confidence among the hazards used.
- **Weather-stat answers:** based on data coverage (≥ 95% of days = High).
- **Out-of-scope answers:** `null`.

The model's own value is always overwritten, and a mismatch is logged.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G7** - **Conversation memory:** the full messages, including tool calls and results, are stored in `chat_messages`. The model sees the **last 10 turns**. That's enough for "why that one?" follow-ups, and it caps token cost.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G8** - **Limits:**
- user message ≤ 1,000 characters
- at most 6 tool steps, then the final answer
- timeouts: 60 s total, 25 s per step, 10 s per tool
- at most 1,500 output tokens
- 1 retry if validation fails

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G9** - **Starting model** (all of these support tools + structured output on OpenRouter today; price per 1M tokens in/out):

| Model | Price | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5` | $2 / $10 | strong at tool use |
| `openai/gpt-6.1-terra` | $1 / $5 | |
| `google/gemini-4-hydrogen` | $1.50 / $7.50 | |
| `anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5` | $0.10 / $0.50 | very cheap |
| `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash` | $0.15 / $0.60 | very cheap |

A rough *estimate* per question: ~25k input + 1k output tokens across steps, which is about **$0.06 on Sonnet** or about **$0.003 on Haiku**. So $20 covers roughly 300 Sonnet questions, and the evals are cheap.

➡️ Start with **`anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`** for reliability while building. The Step 8 bakeoff compares it with GPT-6.1-terra, Gemini-4-hydrogen and Haiku-5.5.

---

❓ **G10** - **Testing the agent:**
- **Unit tests** use the AI SDK's **mock model** (`ai/test`) to cover the loop, validation, the retry, the overrides and the premise logic. No real LLM calls, so they're free and repeatable.
- The real LLM is only used in evals (Step 7), plus a dev script, `npm run ask -- "question"`, for manual checks.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G11** - **"Last year" is computed from today's date in code** (current year − 1 = 2025), not hard-coded. Today's date is passed to the model, so the agent stays correct next year too.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **G12** - **The model can't call a tool with an unknown hub.** Tools are built per request, with `hubId` as a Zod **enum of the active hub IDs from the database**, so an invalid ID fails before anything runs. The 36 hubs (ID, name, state, region) are also listed in the instructions, so the model can map "Big D" to `dallas` and answer "Boise isn't one of our hubs."

➡️ Yes.

---

Env for Step 4: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` is already set. Once you answer G9, I'll add `OPENROUTER_MODEL` to `.env.local` and `.env.example`, and the drift test will make sure it stays documented.

Thanks. All of G1 and G3–G12 are agreed. **G2's unit switch is a good idea**, and it raises one follow-up that's yours to decide:

❓ **G2b** - **What the unit switch changes.** Tools always return both systems, so anything *the code* draws can flip instantly: data panels, charts, widgets. The **answer text** is different. The model writes it, so its units are fixed once it's written. Options:
- **(a)** The switch (US / Metric, saved in the browser) **flips every data panel and chart instantly**, and also tells the agent which system to lead with from the **next answer on**. Past answer text stays as it was written.
- **(b)** Same, but flipping it also **re-asks the last question** to re-render that text. That costs one extra LLM call per flip and could reword the answer.

➡️ (a). It's cheap, predictable, and the text always includes the other unit in brackets anyway, e.g. "6 in (15 cm)".

---

Under NWS definitions, snowfall below 0.1 inch counts as a trace rather than a measurable amount. The NWS forecast matrix guide treats frozen precipitation under 0.1 inch as unmeasurable, labeling it a trace and showing it as "T."

For observers, the NWS snow measurement guidelines call for measuring snowfall to the nearest 0.1 inch. If snow melts as it falls and never builds to 0.1 inch on the measuring surface, the observer records a trace and notes in the remarks that the snow melted as it landed.

Snow depth on the ground follows a different rule. Per the NWS spotter guidance, a snow depth under one-half inch is reported as a trace.

A caveat: a separate NOAA MADIS page sets a much smaller threshold, treating values under 0.001 inches as a trace when reporting to 1-inch precision. That appears to apply to a coarser reporting context, so the 0.1-inch rule is the one that matters for standard snowfall observations.

content.text:
Found the root cause. It isn't a parsing bug, it's the **output limit from G8**:

```text
step 1–6: explain_hub_score, rank_hubs, explain_hub_score, get_weather_stat ×2, explain_hub_score
step 7:   finish=length · 1,500 tokens   ← the 1,500-token cap cut the JSON off mid-way
          {"answer":"**Dallas is rated High, and the data supports that.** Its overall score is 72.4…
           …{"label":"extreme-heat days in 2025","value     ← truncated
```

The answer itself was good: it checked the premise and correctly said "Dallas is rated High, and the data supports that. 72.4, rank 3 of 36". It just ran out of room. Two causes:
1. **The answer JSON is long.** The model copied lots of numbers into `dataUsed` and repeated standing caveats in `limitations`, which code adds automatically anyway.
2. **The model over-explored:** 6 tool calls, 3 of them the same `explain_hub_score`. That's slow and costs more, because each step resends the whole context.

❓ **G14** - **Fixing the truncation** (this changes the G8 limit you agreed to, so it's your call):
- **(a) Tighten the output (no limit change):**
  - schema caps: `dataUsed` ≤ 12 key numbers, `limitations` only for caveats *specific to this answer* (code adds the standing ones), answer text ~250 words max
  - one prompt line: "1–3 tool calls are usually enough; don't call the same tool twice with the same input"
- **(b) Also raise `maxOutputTokens` from 1,500 to 3,000**, as headroom so a long comparison doesn't fail. It costs nothing unless it's used.

➡️ **(a) + (b).** (a) fixes the cause, (b) is a safety margin. Then I'll re-run the Dallas question, plus the other three brief questions, and show you the answers, token counts and timings.

Still open from earlier: **G13** (does "had snowfall" mean measurable snow ≥ 0.1 in, which gives 9.0% for Denver in 2025?). The Denver question needs that answer.

I read "1+b" as **G14: (a) + (b)**: tighten the output (it fixes cause 1) *and* raise the cap to 3,000. If you meant something else, tell me and I'll adjust. I'll ask G13 again at the end, since the Denver question depends on it.

### Agent details (Step 4, round G1–G14)
| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D59 | **Tool contracts** (G1): `rank_hubs` (metric, region?, order, limit → score, level, **rank among all 36**), `compare_hubs` (2–5 hubs, hazards? → both halves + confidence), `get_weather_stat` (hub, metric, year/month, range or last 12 months → count, % of days with data, coverage), `explain_hub_score` (full breakdown with the formula **and its numbers**). | Matches the brief's question types. The formula string is built by code, so the model never does arithmetic. |
| D60 | **Units** (G2, G2b): tools return thresholds in both systems, converted **in code**. Answers lead with the user's system and put the other in brackets. A **US/Metric switch** in the UI flips data panels and charts instantly and sets the system for new answers. Past answer text stays as written. | US analysts first, but not everyone uses US units. The LLM never converts numbers. Re-asking on every flip would cost money and could change wording. |
| D61 | **"The LLM never invents numbers", enforced** (G3): every `dataUsed` value must match a number a tool returned (allowing display rounding), or the answer fails → one retry → clear error. Numbers in the free text that no tool returned are **logged as warnings**, not blocked. | Hard-checking structured data is reliable. Hard-checking prose would misfire on years, "5-year window" and so on. |
| D62 | **Standing caveats are guaranteed by code** (G4), in one file (`scoring/caveats.ts`), built from the config thresholds. The model can add limitations but can't drop ours. | Honesty over precision (D20b), enforced rather than hoped for. |
| D63 | **The premise verdict is decided by code** (G5): the model only extracts the claim (hub, hazard, claimed level). Code compares it with the real level. | "Why is Seattle's hurricane risk high?" gets corrected by data, not by the model's judgment. |
| D64 | **Answer confidence by code** (G6): the weakest confidence of the data used. Weather stats use coverage. Out-of-scope or data-free answers get none. | Same principle as D21. |
| D65 | **Memory** (G7): the last **10 turns**, including tool results. Follow-ups may reuse numbers from **earlier tool results in the same conversation**, so the validator trusts those too. | The first live follow-up was wrongly rejected (the validator only trusted the current turn), which forced a needless retry. Fixed test-first. |

Answers are capped at ~250 words and ≤ 12 `dataUsed` numbers. Model limitations are answer-specific only. # Assumptions, uncertainty & scope

What this agent assumes, what it can't know, and what it deliberately doesn't do.
The agent repeats the relevant parts in its answers (the `assumptions` and `limitations` fields).

## What the score means and doesn't mean
- **It measures exposure, not loss.** It shows how often hazardous weather hits a hub's location. It does
  **not** include hub volume or revenue, building quality, existing resilience upgrades, insurance,
  or how well the local area copes. "Most exposed" ≠ "most expensive".
- **Local adaptation is not modeled.** The same 5 cm of snow paralyzes Atlanta but not Minneapolis.
  We use one national threshold per hazard (an absolute scale). Southern cold and ice exposure is partly covered by
  FEMA's ice storm and cold wave frequencies. *Later:* per-hub local thresholds.
- **All hubs are treated as equally important.** We have no shipment or revenue data. *Later:* optional volume weighting.
- Scores are **decision support**. Final investment decisions belong to the team.

## Location
- A hub = the metro's **city-center point**. Real warehouses often sit near the airport or on the metro's edge,
  possibly in a different county.
- Weather is read for that point from a ~9–11 km model grid. FEMA data is for the **county** that contains the point.

## Data sources & their limits
| Source | Used for | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| [Open-Meteo Historical Weather API](https://open-meteo.com/en/docs/historical-weather-api) | Daily snowfall, min temperature, precipitation, max wind gust, max apparent temperature, 2021-01-01 → yesterday, in each hub's local calendar day | It's **modeled reanalysis, not station measurements**: it smooths peaks, so wind gusts in particular are underestimated. The last few days are **preliminary** and get revised, so we re-fetch the last 7 every night. The free tier is **non-commercial**: a real deployment needs a paid plan. Data is licensed CC-BY 4.0 (attribution shown in the UI). |
| [FEMA National Risk Index v1.20 (Dec 2025)](https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/data-resources) via its public [ArcGIS county service](https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Counties/FeatureServer/0) | Annualized frequency of hurricane, tornado, hail, inland and coastal flooding, ice storm, winter weather, cold wave, heat wave, strong wind | County-level. Built from long historical records, so it **changes slowly** and won't reflect last year's events. Riverine flood is now called `IFLD` (Inland Flooding). |

## Known scoring limitations (Step 3)
How these are handled is in [decisions.md](decisions.md) D47–D58. The numbers are in
[`src/core/scoring/config.ts`](../src/core/scoring/config.ts).
- **County-level FEMA data depends on county shape and size.**
  - **Tornado:** FEMA spreads frequency by county area (within-state rank correlation +0.62), so we score **per 1,000 sq mi** (D53).
  - **Inland flood:** a mild size effect (+0.21) that we do not correct. Huge counties (Maricopa/Phoenix 9,319 sq mi, Clark/Las Vegas,
    Los Angeles) likely have an overstated FEMA flood half.
  - **Mountains:** King County (Seattle) includes the Cascades and Salt Lake County the Wasatch, which inflates FEMA winter weather.
    Seattle's winter is flagged **Medium confidence** because the sources disagree (D52).
- **The FEMA flood half caps at 100 for 15 of 36 hubs** (metros issue many flood warnings), so FEMA alone can't separate
  them. The observed half still does. **To revisit in Step 7** (D57).
- **Heavy rain ≠ flooding.** The flood score blends heavy-rain days with FEMA's flood warnings but doesn't cross-check them (D56).
- **Ice storms come from FEMA only.** Observed weather has no ice signal (D56).
- **Heavy-snow days (≥15 cm) and warning-level gusts (≥93 km/h) are reported, not scored.** The modeled data barely
  registers them (D20a, D50).
- **FEMA anchors are national 95th percentiles** among counties where FEMA rates the hazard. Coastal flooding is
  rated for only 588 coastal counties, so its anchor compares coastal counties with each other (D47).
- **Heat:** FEMA heat waves follow local NWS heat-alert criteria (lower thresholds up north), while our observed heat days
  use one national ≥40 °C feels-like threshold. Disagreement there is real and is flagged (e.g. New York, Kansas City).

## Time window
- Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest available day, so they move slightly every night.
- "Last year" means **calendar 2025** unless the user says otherwise. The agent states the period it used.
- 5 years is short for rare events (hurricanes, big ice storms). That's why those rely on FEMA's long-record frequencies.

## Thresholds (checked against US National Weather Service criteria)
NWS sets most warning criteria **per local office**, so there is rarely one national number. We picked one
national value per hazard, close to typical NWS warning levels:

| Day type | Our threshold | NWS reference | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snow day | ≥ 1 cm snowfall | No NWS daily definition | A reasonable "measurable snow" proxy |
| Heavy snow day | ≥ 15 cm (~6 in) | Winter Storm Warning: locally set, roughly 4–12 in ([NWSI 10-513](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005013curr.pdf), [criteria map](https://www.weather.gov/snow-criteria)). Denver: 6 in/12 h ([BOU](https://www.weather.gov/bou/winterguide)) | Southern offices use lower values |
| Extreme cold day | min temp ≤ −18 °C (0 °F) | Extreme Cold Warning (replaced Wind Chill Warning on 2024-10-01, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/243009-cold-hazard-simplification)). Locally set, from about 0 °F (South) to −35 °F (North) | Uses air temperature, not wind chill |
| Heavy rain day | ≥ 50 mm (~2 in) | **No NWS daily rain threshold**: flood warnings are impact-based. NOAA tracks heavy days as the top 1% locally ([USGCRP](https://www.globalchange.gov/indicators/heavy-precipitation)) | Arid hubs rarely reach 50 mm. Their flash-flood exposure comes through FEMA |
| High wind day | gust ≥ 93 km/h (58 mph) | High Wind Warning: sustained ≥ 40 mph or gusts ≥ 58 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)) | Exact match |
| Wind advisory day | gust ≥ 72 km/h (45 mph) | Wind Advisory: sustained 30–39 mph (NWSI 10-515). The 45 mph gust value is our own choice | **The wind signal we actually score on.** The Step 2 check over 5 years: warning-level days were 0–1/yr (13 of 36 hubs at 0, because modeled data smooths peaks, though single storms do show up, e.g. Tampa 153 km/h during Hurricane Milton), while advisory days were 0.2–8.6/yr |
| Extreme heat day | apparent temp max ≥ 40 °C (~105 °F) | Extreme Heat Warning (renamed from Excessive Heat Warning 2025-03-04, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/250310-heat-hazard)): heat index ~105–110 °F, locally set | Open-Meteo's "apparent temperature" is a different formula from the NWS heat index |

## Out of scope (Phase 1)
- **Dust storms.** FEMA has no dust hazard. NOAA's [Storm Events Database](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/)
  has "Dust Storm" events by forecast zone (84 nationwide in 2023, mostly TX/AZ/CA). Dust storm warning criteria:
  visibility ≤ ¼ mile with winds usually ≥ 25 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)).
  Planned as the first post-deploy feature.
- Wildfire smoke, earthquakes, lightning and drought (FEMA has some of these, but they aren't weather-disruption
  hazards in our brief).
- Forecasts and live alerts. Phase 1 is historical exposure only.
- Cities that aren't in our hub list. The agent says so instead of guessing.

## Operational limits of the demo deployment
- The OpenRouter key has a **$20 credit cap** and **expires 7 days after creation (around 2026-12-02)**.
  After that the agent can't answer until a new key is set in Vercel's environment variables.
- Open-Meteo's free tier is per-IP and non-commercial. A production version needs their paid API.

## Uncertainty the agent communicates
- **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed in code from data completeness (≥95% of days present) and
  the number of sources backing each hazard (observed + FEMA).
- Every answer lists the assumptions and limitations that apply to it.

# 🦉 The Daily Prophet

A weather risk intelligence agent for a logistics company's US distribution hubs.
Analysts chat with it to find out which hubs are most exposed to severe weather, compare hubs,
and understand *why* a hub is risky, to help decide where to invest in resilience upgrades.

> 🚧 Work in progress. Built step by step. See [docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md).

## Docs
- [Plan](docs/plan.md): architecture, tables, steps
- [Decision log](docs/decisions.md): every choice and why
- [Assumptions, uncertainty & scope](docs/assumptions.md)
- [Design](docs/design.md)
- [AI session log](docs/session/): the full conversation with the coding agent

## Run locally
Requirements: Node 22+, a Supabase project.

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local     # then fill in the values (see comments in the file)
npm run db:check               # verifies the database connection: lists the hubs
npm run dev                    # http://localhost:3000
```

## Scripts
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` | Start the app locally |
| `npm test` | Unit tests (Vitest) |
| `npm run typecheck` | TypeScript check |
| `npm run lint` | ESLint (includes the rule keeping `src/core` free of Next.js) |
| `npm run db:check` | Connect to Supabase and list hubs per region |
| `npm run ingest` | Fetch FEMA + Open-Meteo data for all active hubs (incremental; the first full load takes about 1 h because of Open-Meteo's rate limits) |
| `npm run ingest -- --hub=dallas,denver` | Same, for selected hubs only |
| `npm run ingest -- --refresh-fema` | Re-fetch FEMA records for every hub (e.g. after a new NRI release) |
| `npm run score` | Re-score all hubs from stored data (no API calls). The ingest runs this automatically. |
| `npm run fema:anchors` | Recompute the national 95th-percentile FEMA anchors (for review before changing `scoring/config.ts`) |
| `npm run session:export -- <file.jsonl>` | Export the AI session log to `docs/session/` (scrubbed) |

## Database
SQL migrations live in [supabase/migrations/](supabase/migrations/). Apply them in order to a fresh
Supabase project (SQL editor or Supabase CLI). The second migration seeds the 36 hubs.

## Data attribution
Weather data by [Open-Meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com/) (CC BY 4.0). Hazard data: FEMA National Risk Index.

@AGENTS.md

# The Daily Prophet: project rules

A weather-risk agent for logistics hubs (take-home assignment). Read before any work:
[docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md) for architecture and the step list, [docs/decisions.md](docs/decisions.md)
for every agreed choice and its reason, and [docs/assumptions.md](docs/assumptions.md) for data limits.

## Teamwork: decide together
Yarden and Claude are one team. Decisions are made together, not by Claude alone.
- **Ask first** about anything that changes product behavior, data or its meaning, architecture,
  dependencies, DB schema, scoring, or what users see. Give a recommendation, then wait.
- **Do and log** the mechanical things: naming inside a function, test structure, formatting, type fixes.
- **Unsure which?** Ask.
- Every agreed decision goes into `docs/decisions.md` in plain language ("What / Why").
  Assumptions and data limits go into `docs/assumptions.md`.

## Workflow
- Small steps. One branch and one PR per step. Yarden reviews and merges. Claude never merges or pushes to `main`.
- After each step: say what was done and what's next, then wait for an OK.
- Before each step: list the `.env` variables it will need.
- PR bodies explain the decisions made and the evidence (test output, data checks).
- Refresh the session log with `npm run session:export`. Its built-in leak check must pass before the log is committed.

## Before writing code
1. **Reuse.** Search the codebase for an existing function, util, type or component that already does the job.
2. **Usages.** Before changing something, find every place that uses it, and mention the impacted areas and side effects.
3. **Single source of truth.** Each fact lives in one place. Derive what can be derived. If you see the same
   state, config or schema in two places, flag it before coding. When a copy is unavoidable (e.g. a DB
   constraint mirrored in a TS type), a test must fail when they drift.
4. **Fewest moving parts.** Between plans with the same outcome, pick the one with fewer things that can fail
   (network calls, manual steps, multi-step migrations, parallel writes).

## Code rules
- **`src/core/` stays framework-free:** no Next.js or React imports (enforced by ESLint).
- **JSDoc** on every exported and internal function, class, method and type. Explain clearly and simply.
- **Errors.** Wrap every boundary operation (external API, DB, LLM, Jev, API route, script entry point) in
  try/catch and rethrow as `BoundaryError` (`src/core/errors/boundaryError.ts`), which formats
  `ErrorName || message || functionName || emoji` with a fixed emoji per boundary. Pure functions (scoring,
  stats, parsing) throw plain errors and leave formatting to the boundary. When you deliberately continue
  after an error, log it in the same format.
- **Timeouts on every external call, no exceptions.** HTTP: `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` (or an
  `AbortController`). Supabase: the client's wrapped `fetch`. LLM calls: the AI SDK timeout/abort option.
- **Secrets** live only in `.env.local` (local) and Vercel env vars (prod). `.env.example` lists every variable.
- **After every migration:** regenerate `src/core/db/database.types.ts` from the live schema.
- **The LLM never produces numbers.** Scores and stats come from tested TypeScript, and the LLM picks tools and explains.

## Honesty
- **Verify before claiming.** Before saying a file, function, table, column, env var, package, endpoint,
  command or flag exists, check it: read the file, grep the symbol, query the schema, run `--help`.
  When unsure, say so explicitly.
- **Honesty over precision** for end users too: when our data measures something poorly, the agent says so
  plainly instead of presenting a weak number as fact.
- Be candid with Yarden: criticize plans and code, including your own, when something is wrong.

## Vibes
Love cats 🐱. Use cat emojis in chat and UI copy where they fit 😸. Error-boundary emojis stay as defined in
`boundaryError.ts`.

## Hard-won lessons
Each one: *next time you see X → do Y*.
1. **`npm run x -- --flag` on PowerShell** → the `--` is swallowed and the flag arrives as env var
   `npm_config_flag`. Read both `process.argv` and `process.env.npm_config_*`.
2. **"This API probably lags N days / returns shape X"** → probe the real API first. Open-Meteo's archive
   served data up to yesterday, not 5 days back as assumed.
3. **Supabase pause fails with "hibernating"** → it can't be paused through the API. Ask Yarden to pause it in
   the dashboard.
4. **A long Bash heredoc fails with "unexpected EOF"** → write files with the Write tool.
5. **Weather data shows (near) zero extreme events** → check whether reanalysis smoothing is hiding the peaks
   before concluding "safe". Gusts ≥93 km/h were 0–1/yr even in windy hubs, so we score on ≥72 km/h.
6. **"Untracked working tree files would be overwritten" after switching to an older `main`** → compare file
   hashes against the target commit before any reset. The files were identical and nothing was lost.
7. **Vitest is green** → still run `npm run typecheck`. Vitest strips types without checking them. A wrong field
   name (`reason` vs `confidenceReason`) passed every test and was only caught by `tsc`.
8. **Reading more than 1,000 rows from Supabase** → paginate with `.range()`. PostgREST caps each response at
   1,000 rows by default and silently returns the first page (a 1,826-day window would have been cut off).
9. **A rule-based label fires on almost everything (32 of 36 hubs "Medium")** → check whether it's flagging
   *structural* differences (two sources that measure different things) rather than real problems. Compare like with like (D56).

## Summary

Step 4 of [the plan](docs/plan.md): **the agent.** The LLM picks tools and writes the explanation. **Code computes every number and checks the answer**, then sets the premise verdict, confidence, caveats and disclaimer itself. All four example questions from the brief work live.

```text
answerQuestion({ sessionId, message, units })        # src/core/agent/answerQuestion.ts — the one entry point
  ensureSession · loadHistory (last 10 turns)        # Supabase chat_sessions / chat_messages
  loadAgentContext                                   # hubs + latest snapshots + data bounds, once per request
  runAgent
    ledger.seedFromHistory                           # earlier tool results count as known numbers (D65)
    streamText(tools, Output.object(llmAnswerSchema), stopWhen 7 steps, timeouts, ≤3,000 tokens)
      tools: rank_hubs · compare_hubs · get_weather_stat · explain_hub_score
        runTool → onToolStart/onToolEnd → ledger.record
      partialOutputStream → onAnswerDelta            # answer text streams as it's written
    finalizeAnswer(raw, ledger)
      hard:  hubsMentioned ⊆ tool hubs · dataUsed numbers ∈ tool numbers · recommendation needs data
      code:  premiseCheck.holds · confidence · + standing caveats · + disclaimer
      soft:  numbers in prose not returned by tools → warnings
    invalid → send problems back → retry once → AgentAnswerValidationError (🦉)
  saveTurn · recordEvent(agent.answered | agent.retry | agent.failed)
```

```text
src/core/agent/          answerQuestion · runAgent · finalizeAnswer · ledger · answerSchema · systemPrompt · context · model · config
src/core/agent/tools/    rankHubs · compareHubs · explainHubScore · getWeatherStat · shared · index
src/core/scoring/        dayMetrics (ONE definition of each hazard day) · caveats · ranking (+ types now Zod schemas)
src/core/stats/          weatherStats (periods + counts)
src/core/utils/units.ts  conversions in code, never by the LLM
src/core/db/             chatRepository · scoresRepository.getLatestSnapshots · weatherRepository.getWeatherBounds
scripts/ask.ts           npm run ask -- "question" [--session=<id>] [--metric]
```

## Decisions (D59–D72, round G1–G14)

| # | Decision |
|---|---|
| D59 | Tool contracts (G1). Ranks among all 36 hubs. The formula string is built by code |
| D60 | Units converted in code. US first, metric in brackets. A US/Metric switch flips panels instantly and sets new answers (G2, G2b) |
| D61 | `dataUsed` numbers must trace to tools (hard). Numbers in the prose are soft warnings (G3) |
| D62 | Standing caveats guaranteed by code, built from config (G4) |
| D63 | **Premise verdict by code**. The model only extracts the claim (G5) |
| D64 | Answer confidence by code (G6) |
| D65 | Memory: last 10 turns. The validator **trusts earlier tool results** (G7, plus a fix found live) |
| D66 | Limits, with **3,000 output tokens** (raised from 1,500), answers ≤ ~250 words, ≤ 12 numbers (G8, G14) |
| D67 | Start on `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`. Bakeoff in Step 8 (G9) |
| D68 | Agent loop unit-tested with the AI SDK mock model (G10) |
| D69 | "Last year" from today's date. Hub ids are a Zod enum of active hubs (G11, G12) |
| D70 | One shared hazard-day definition for scoring and stats |
| D71 | One entry point, `answerQuestion`, with `agent.*` events |
| D72 | "Had snowfall" = **measurable snow ≥ 0.1 in (NWS)**, reported alongside the scored ≥ 0.4 in figure (G13) |

## Evidence

**Tests:** `Test Files 28 passed · Tests 138 passed`. Type check, lint and build are clean. Agent-loop tests use `MockLanguageModelV4`:
- tool call, then the answer is streamed, then code checks it
- an invented number gets a retry, then succeeds
- two bad answers produce `AgentAnswerValidationError || … || runAgent || 🦉`
- a follow-up reuses history without a retry
- an over-long message is rejected before any model call

**Live runs** (`npm run ask`, Sonnet 5.5):

| Question | Answer (abridged) | Tools · time · tokens in/out |
|---|---|---|
| Why is the Dallas hub's risk high? *(brief)* | "Yes, Dallas is rated High. 72.4 (High starts at 67), 3rd of 36. Overall = 0.6 × 54 + 0.4 × 100." Premise: high → high ✔ | 2 · 19 s · 26.7k/1.3k |
| Which Midwest hubs are most exposed to winter? *(brief)* | Minneapolis 86.5 (#2 of 36), Detroit 70.3 (#3). Both High | 2 · 12 s · 22.0k/1.2k |
| Compare Miami and Houston, hurricane + flood *(brief)* | Miami leads hurricane 100 vs 74. Houston leads flood 84 vs 76, with the reason it leads | 1 · 17 s · 21.4k/1.2k |
| % of days in Denver last year with snowfall? *(brief)* | "About 9%: 33 of 365 days ≥ 0.1 in. Our score's stricter bar: 17 days, 4.7%." | 3 · 16 s · 21.4k/1.2k |
| Follow-up: which of those two to prioritize? | Leans slightly Houston (broader risk), Miami if the upgrade is hurricane-specific. Code-added disclaimer | 32 s, had a retry (bug, now fixed) |
| Follow-up: remind me their hurricane scores | 100 and 74 from memory, **no retry** after the fix | 1 · 9 s |
| Why is Seattle's hurricane risk so high? | "**Seattle's hurricane risk is not high. It is low.**" Premise: high → low ✘ | 5 · 21 s · 61.4k/1.7k |
| Write me a poem about cats | Polite decline, `outOfScope: true` | 0 · 5 s · 6.2k/0.2k |

**Bugs the live runs exposed, all fixed test-first:**
1. The first answer was cut off at the 1,500-token cap (`finish=length`). Fixed with G14 and recorded as lesson #10.
2. The validator rejected numbers from earlier turns in the same conversation. Fixed with D65 and lesson #12.
3. "0-100" was read as the numbers 0 and −100. Fixed with a range-dash-aware regex and scale bounds treated as known.

**Known, for Step 7/8:**
- The model sometimes calls more tools than needed (5 for Seattle).
- Input tokens grow with conversation length (~35k by the third turn).
- About 14 limitations per answer (the UI will collapse them).

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

No schema change. New tables already existed (`chat_*`). The only refactor is that `observedSignals` now uses the shared `dayMetrics`. Its 44 existing tests stayed green unchanged.

**Blast Radius:** small

New modules. Scoring output is unchanged.

## Env vars

- `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`: already set
- `OPENROUTER_MODEL=anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`: added to `.env.example` and `.env.local`

Both are covered by the `.env.example` drift test.

## Next: Step 5 (API)

The step adds:
- a streaming `POST /api/chat` that wraps `answerQuestion`
- `/api/widgets`
- a protected `/api/cron/ingest` that runs `runIngestThenScore`
- Basic Auth in `proxy.ts`

It needs `APP_USERNAME`, `APP_PASSWORD` and `CRON_SECRET`.

I have the facts I need: the route-handler pattern, `createUIMessageStream` / `writer.write({ type: 'data-…' })`, `transient` data parts, and `createUIMessageStreamResponse`. All three env values are set.

## Step 5: the API, short question round
Most of Step 5 was settled in round 1 (Q12, Q13, Q16, Q11). These are the remaining details:

❓ **A1** - **What `/api/chat` streams**, using the AI SDK chat protocol (D26):

| Event | When | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `data-session` | first | the session ID the browser stores |
| `data-progress` (one per tool call, updated in place) | tool starts / finishes | "Explaining Dallas's score… ✓" |
| text deltas | while the model writes | the answer appearing live |
| `data-retry` | the answer failed validation | the UI clears the draft and shows "re-checking…" |
| `data-answer` | end | the **validated** final answer (data panel, confidence, caveats, recommendation) |
| `error` | failure | a short, friendly message |

Request body (Zod-validated): `{ sessionId: uuid | null, message: string, units: "us" | "metric" }`.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **A2** - **Auth in two layers.** Next 16's own docs say proxy "should not be used as a full… authorization solution". So:
1. `src/proxy.ts` does Basic Auth on every page and API route except `/api/cron/*`.
2. Each API route **checks again** using the same small function.

The username/password comparison is constant-time, so the password can't be guessed by measuring response times. The cron route accepts only `Authorization: Bearer <CRON_SECRET>`, which Vercel sends automatically.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **A3** - **Nightly job schedule:** `0 6 * * *` = **06:00 UTC** (about 1–2 a.m. US Eastern). Open-Meteo already has yesterday's data by then, and Hobby-plan cron fires sometime within that hour. The job runs the same `runIngestThenScore` pipeline as `npm run ingest`, with a 300 s limit. Last measured: about 60 s.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **A4** - **Error responses:** `{ error: { code, message } }`, with friendly text and no internals. Full details go to the server log in the `Name || message || fn || emoji` format, and to `events`.

| Case | Status | Code |
|---|---|---|
| bad input, message too long | 400 | `invalid_request` |
| wrong or missing credentials | 401 | `unauthorized` |
| no data ingested yet | 503 | `no_data` |
| model failed or answered invalidly twice | 502 | `agent_failed` |
| anything else | 500 | `internal_error` |

During streaming, errors arrive as the `error` event, with the same friendly text.

➡️ Yes.

---

❓ **A5** - **`/api/widgets`** returns:
- top 5 hubs by overall score
- the leading hub for each of the 6 hazards
- data status (weather through date, number of hubs, when last scored, scoring version, FEMA version)

It's computed by a pure, tested function from the latest snapshots, with no LLM. No public `/api/health` route for now: one route fewer, and the evals can hit `/api/chat` directly.

➡️ Yes.

---
title: Route Segment Config
description: Learn about how to configure options for Next.js route segments.
---
The Route Segment Config options allow you to configure the behavior of a [Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), [Layout](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout), or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) by directly exporting the following variables:
| Option                                                                                             | Type                                                              | Default                    |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| [`dynamicParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/dynamicParams)     | `boolean`                                                         | `true`                     |
| [`runtime`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/runtime)                 | `'nodejs' \| 'edge' (deprecated)`                                 | `'nodejs'`                 |
| [`preferredRegion`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/preferredRegion) | `'auto' \| 'global' \| 'home' \| string \| string[] (deprecated)` | `'auto'`                   |
| [`maxDuration`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/maxDuration)         | `number`                                                          | Set by deployment platform |
With [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) enabled, pages and layouts also support the following option:
| Option                                                                                       | Type                                                               | Default  |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- |
| [`ensureStatic`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/ensureStatic) | `'auto'` \| `'shell'` \| `'prefetch'` \| `'navigation'` \| `false` | `'auto'` |
## Version History
| Version      |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `v16.0.0`    | `dynamic`, `dynamicParams`, `revalidate`, and `fetchCache` removed when [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled. See [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components#route-segment-config). |
| `v16.0.0`    | `export const experimental_ppr = true` removed. A [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#remove-experimental_ppr-route-segment-config-from-app-router-pages-and-layouts) is available.                                                                                                  |
| `v15.0.0-RC` | `export const runtime = "experimental-edge"` deprecated. A [codemod](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/codemods#transform-app-router-route-segment-config-runtime-value-from-experimental-edge-to-edge) is available.                                                                                 |
---
title: maxDuration
description: API reference for the maxDuration route segment config option.
---
The `maxDuration` option allows you to set the maximum execution time (in seconds) for server-side logic in a route segment. Deployment platforms can use `maxDuration` from the Next.js build output to add specific execution limits.
```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx | route.ts" switcher
export const maxDuration = 5
```
```js filename="layout.js | page.js | route.js" switcher
export const maxDuration = 5
```
## Server Actions
If using [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data), set the `maxDuration` at the page level to change the default timeout of all Server Actions used on the page.
## Version History
| Version    | Changes                   |

title: maxDuration
description: API reference for the maxDuration route segment config option.
---
The `maxDuration` option allows you to set the maximum execution time (in seconds) for server-side logic in a route segment. Deployment platforms can use `maxDuration` from the Next.js build output to add specific execution limits.

```

```

If using [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data), set the `maxDuration` at the page level to change the default timeout of all Server Actions used on the page.

The final cutoff will be tuned on eval data. More abuse protection is planned later. |

### API details (Step 5, round A1–A5)
| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D73 | **`POST /api/chat` streams the AI SDK chat protocol** (A1): `data-session` first, then `data-progress` (one per tool call, updated in place, with friendly labels like "Breaking down Dallas's risk score…"), then answer text deltas, `data-retry` if validation failed (the UI drops the draft), and finally `data-answer` (validated) **or** `data-error`. Body: `{ sessionId \| null, message, units }`, Zod-validated. | The UI can show live progress *and* only trust the validated answer. The stream builder lives in `src/core/api` so it's unit-tested without Next.js. |
| D74 | **Two auth layers** (A2): `src/proxy.ts` (Basic Auth on everything except `/api/cron` and static assets) **plus** a re-check inside every API route, using one constant-time function (`core/security/auth.ts`). # The Daily Prophet: project rules

A weather-risk agent for logistics hubs (take-home assignment). Read before any work:
[docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md) for architecture and the step list, [docs/decisions.md](docs/decisions.md)
for every agreed choice and its reason, and [docs/assumptions.md](docs/assumptions.md) for data limits.

## Teamwork: decide together
Yarden and Claude are one team. Decisions are made together, not by Claude alone.
- **Ask first** about anything that changes product behavior, data or its meaning, architecture,
  dependencies, DB schema, scoring, or what users see. Give a recommendation, then wait.
- **Do and log** the mechanical things: naming inside a function, test structure, formatting, type fixes.
- **Unsure which?** Ask.
- Every agreed decision goes into `docs/decisions.md` in plain language ("What / Why").
  Assumptions and data limits go into `docs/assumptions.md`.

## Workflow
- Small steps. One branch and one PR per step. Yarden reviews and merges. Claude never merges or pushes to `main`.
- After each step: say what was done and what's next, then wait for an OK.
- Before each step: list the `.env` variables it will need.
- PR bodies explain the decisions made and the evidence (test output, data checks).
- Refresh the session log with `npm run session:export`. Its built-in leak check must pass before the log is committed.

## Before writing code
1. **Reuse.** Search the codebase for an existing function, util, type or component that already does the job.
2. **Usages.** Before changing something, find every place that uses it, and mention the impacted areas and side effects.
3. **Single source of truth.** Each fact lives in one place. Derive what can be derived. If you see the same
   state, config or schema in two places, flag it before coding. When a copy is unavoidable (e.g. a DB
   constraint mirrored in a TS type), a test must fail when they drift.
4. **Fewest moving parts.** Between plans with the same outcome, pick the one with fewer things that can fail
   (network calls, manual steps, multi-step migrations, parallel writes).

## Code rules
- **`src/core/` stays framework-free:** no Next.js or React imports (enforced by ESLint).
- **JSDoc** on every exported and internal function, class, method and type. Explain clearly and simply.
- **Errors.** Wrap every boundary operation (external API, DB, LLM, Jev, API route, script entry point) in
  try/catch and rethrow as `BoundaryError` (`src/core/errors/boundaryError.ts`), which formats
  `ErrorName || message || functionName || emoji` with a fixed emoji per boundary. Pure functions (scoring,
  stats, parsing) throw plain errors and leave formatting to the boundary. When you deliberately continue
  after an error, log it in the same format.
- **Timeouts on every external call, no exceptions.** HTTP: `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` (or an
  `AbortController`). Supabase: the client's wrapped `fetch`. LLM calls: the AI SDK timeout/abort option.
- **Secrets** live only in `.env.local` (local) and Vercel env vars (prod). `.env.example` lists every variable.
- **After every migration:** regenerate `src/core/db/database.types.ts` from the live schema.
- **The LLM never produces numbers.** Scores and stats come from tested TypeScript, and the LLM picks tools and explains.

## Honesty
- **Verify before claiming.** Before saying a file, function, table, column, env var, package, endpoint,
  command or flag exists, check it: read the file, grep the symbol, query the schema, run `--help`.
  When unsure, say so explicitly.
- **Honesty over precision** for end users too: when our data measures something poorly, the agent says so
  plainly instead of presenting a weak number as fact.
- Be candid with Yarden: criticize plans and code, including your own, when something is wrong.

## Vibes
Love cats 🐱. Use cat emojis in chat and UI copy where they fit 😸. Error-boundary emojis stay as defined in
`boundaryError.ts`.

## Hard-won lessons
Each one: *next time you see X → do Y*.
1. **`npm run x -- --flag` on PowerShell** → the `--` is swallowed and the flag arrives as env var
   `npm_config_flag`. Read both `process.argv` and `process.env.npm_config_*`.
2. **"This API probably lags N days / returns shape X"** → probe the real API first. Open-Meteo's archive
   served data up to yesterday, not 5 days back as assumed.
3. **Supabase pause fails with "hibernating"** → it can't be paused through the API. Ask Yarden to pause it in
   the dashboard.
4. **A long Bash heredoc fails with "unexpected EOF"** → write files with the Write tool.
5. **Weather data shows (near) zero extreme events** → check whether reanalysis smoothing is hiding the peaks
   before concluding "safe". Gusts ≥93 km/h were 0–1/yr even in windy hubs, so we score on ≥72 km/h.
6. **"Untracked working tree files would be overwritten" after switching to an older `main`** → compare file
   hashes against the target commit before any reset. The files were identical and nothing was lost.
7. **Vitest is green** → still run `npm run typecheck`. Vitest strips types without checking them. A wrong field
   name (`reason` vs `confidenceReason`) passed every test and was only caught by `tsc`.
8. **Reading more than 1,000 rows from Supabase** → paginate with `.range()`. PostgREST caps each response at
   1,000 rows by default and silently returns the first page (a 1,826-day window would have been cut off).
9. **A rule-based label fires on almost everything (32 of 36 hubs "Medium")** → check whether it's flagging
   *structural* differences (two sources that measure different things) rather than real problems. Compare like with like (D56).
10. **"No object generated: could not parse the response"** from the AI SDK → inspect each step's
   `finishReason` before blaming the parser. Ours was `length`: the output cap cut the JSON off mid-way.
11. **Writing AI SDK v7 code from memory** → check `node_modules/ai/docs` and the `.d.ts` first. v7 has
   `responseMessages` (not `response.messages`), `isStepCount` (not `stepCountIs`), and `Output.object` alongside tools.
12. **A validator rejects a follow-up's numbers** → check that it trusts the conversation's earlier tool
   results, not just the current turn's (D65).
