- **Heavy-snow days (≥15 cm) and warning-level gusts (≥93 km/h) are reported, not scored.** The modeled data barely
  registers them (D20a, D50).
- **FEMA anchors are national 95th percentiles** among counties where FEMA rates the hazard. Coastal flooding is
  rated for only 588 coastal counties, so its anchor compares coastal counties with each other (D47).
- **Heat:** FEMA heat waves follow local NWS heat-alert criteria (lower thresholds up north), while our observed heat days
  use one national ≥40 °C feels-like threshold. Disagreement there is real and is flagged (e.g. New York, Kansas City).

## Time window
- Scores use a **rolling 5-year window** ending at the newest available day, so they move slightly every night.
- "Last year" means **calendar 2025** unless the user says otherwise. The agent states the period it used.
- 5 years is short for rare events (hurricanes, big ice storms). That's why those rely on FEMA's long-record frequencies.

## Thresholds (checked against US National Weather Service criteria)
NWS sets most warning criteria **per local office**, so there is rarely one national number. We picked one
national value per hazard, close to typical NWS warning levels:

| Day type | Our threshold | NWS reference | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snow day | ≥ 1 cm snowfall | No NWS daily definition | A reasonable "measurable snow" proxy |
| Heavy snow day | ≥ 15 cm (~6 in) | Winter Storm Warning: locally set, roughly 4–12 in ([NWSI 10-513](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005013curr.pdf), [criteria map](https://www.weather.gov/snow-criteria)). Denver: 6 in/12 h ([BOU](https://www.weather.gov/bou/winterguide)) | Southern offices use lower values |
| Extreme cold day | min temp ≤ −18 °C (0 °F) | Extreme Cold Warning (replaced Wind Chill Warning on 2024-10-01, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/243009-cold-hazard-simplification)). Locally set, from about 0 °F (South) to −35 °F (North) | Uses air temperature, not wind chill |
| Heavy rain day | ≥ 50 mm (~2 in) | **No NWS daily rain threshold**: flood warnings are impact-based. NOAA tracks heavy days as the top 1% locally ([USGCRP](https://www.globalchange.gov/indicators/heavy-precipitation)) | Arid hubs rarely reach 50 mm. Their flash-flood exposure comes through FEMA |
| High wind day | gust ≥ 93 km/h (58 mph) | High Wind Warning: sustained ≥ 40 mph or gusts ≥ 58 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)) | Exact match |
| Wind advisory day | gust ≥ 72 km/h (45 mph) | Wind Advisory: sustained 30–39 mph (NWSI 10-515). The 45 mph gust value is our own choice | **The wind signal we actually score on.** The Step 2 check over 5 years: warning-level days were 0–1/yr (13 of 36 hubs at 0, because modeled data smooths peaks, though single storms do show up, e.g. Tampa 153 km/h during Hurricane Milton), while advisory days were 0.2–8.6/yr |
| Extreme heat day | apparent temp max ≥ 40 °C (~105 °F) | Extreme Heat Warning (renamed from Excessive Heat Warning 2025-03-04, [NWS](https://www.weather.gov/news/250310-heat-hazard)): heat index ~105–110 °F, locally set | Open-Meteo's "apparent temperature" is a different formula from the NWS heat index |

## Out of scope (Phase 1)
- **Dust storms.** FEMA has no dust hazard. NOAA's [Storm Events Database](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/swdi/stormevents/csvfiles/)
  has "Dust Storm" events by forecast zone (84 nationwide in 2023, mostly TX/AZ/CA). Dust storm warning criteria:
  visibility ≤ ¼ mile with winds usually ≥ 25 mph ([NWSI 10-515](https://www.weather.gov/media/directives/010_pdfs/pd01005015curr.pdf)).
  Planned as the first post-deploy feature.
- Wildfire smoke, earthquakes, lightning and drought (FEMA has some of these, but they aren't weather-disruption
  hazards in our brief).
- Forecasts and live alerts. Phase 1 is historical exposure only.
- Cities that aren't in our hub list. The agent says so instead of guessing.

## Agent behavior limits (Step 4)
- **Follow-ups may repeat earlier numbers.** Within a conversation, the agent may reuse numbers from earlier
  tool results (D65). If the nightly re-score changed a value since then, a follow-up could repeat the older one.
  Starting a new conversation always uses the latest scores.
- **Free-text numbers are checked softly.** Numbers in `dataUsed` must come from tools (hard check), but numbers
  inside the prose are only *flagged* when no tool returned them (D61). The evals track those warnings.
- **Cost grows with conversation length.** Earlier tool results are sent with each new question, e.g. about 35k
  input tokens by the third turn on Sonnet. The model also sometimes calls more tools than needed (up to 5 for one
  question). Both are measured in the Step 8 bakeoff.

## Operational limits of the demo deployment
- The OpenRouter key has a **$20 credit cap** and **expires 7 days after creation (around 2026-12-02)**.
  After that the agent can't answer until a new key is set in Vercel's environment variables.
- Open-Meteo's free tier is per-IP and non-commercial. A production version needs their paid API.

## Uncertainty the agent communicates
- **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed in code from data completeness (≥95% of days present) and
  the number of sources backing each hazard (observed + FEMA).
- Every answer lists the assumptions and limitations that apply to it.

+> Denver still warrants attention: its severe-storm score is **100**, based on FEMA’s long-term frequency record. If Denver has a particularly vulnerable facility or a more urgent severe-storm upgrade, that could change the priority. These scores are not a forecast for this year.
+Lean toward Houston for the resilience upgrade.
+- Houston’s overall risk score is 69.1, compared with Denver’s 57.9.
+- Houston’s flood, hurricane and heat scores are 84, 74 and 72.6, respectively.
+- Denver’s severe-storm score is 100, so its specific vulnerability remains important.
+- Evidence that Denver’s facility is more vulnerable or operationally critical.
+- Differences in upgrade cost, readiness or expected risk reduction.
+_Disclaimer added by code:_ Decision support based on weather exposure only. It does not include hub volume, upgrade costs or existing resilience. Final decisions belong to your team.
+<details><summary>Numbers it relied on (each one checked against the tool results)</summary>
+- The scores do not forecast hazards for this year; upgrade costs and timing were not provided.
+- Scores measure exposure (how often hazardous weather hits a hub's location), not dollar losses. Hub volume, building condition and existing resilience upgrades are not included.
+- Each hub is its metro's city-center point: weather comes from a ~10 km model grid cell, FEMA data from the county containing that point.
+- Hurricane exposure comes from FEMA's long-term county frequency; any single season can be far above or below it.
+- Heavy-snow days (≥ 5.9 in of snow (≥ 15 cm of snow)) are barely registered by modeled data, so they are reported but not scored.
+- Ice storms come from FEMA only — observed weather has no ice signal.
+- Local adaptation is not modeled: the same snow disrupts southern cities more than northern ones.
+- Heavy-rain days (≥ 2 in of rain (≥ 50 mm of rain)) are not the same as flooding; FEMA's flood frequency counts flood warnings anywhere in the county.
+- In very large counties (e.g. Phoenix, Las Vegas, Los Angeles) FEMA's flood frequency is likely overstated, and for many big metros it is at the top of the scale.
+- Severe storms (tornado + hail) come from FEMA only — five years of daily weather cannot measure them.
+- Tornado frequency is scored per county area, because FEMA spreads tornado frequency by area.
+- Warning-level gusts (gusts ≥ 58 mph (gusts ≥ 93 km/h)) are undercounted by modeled data, so wind is scored on advisory-level gust days (gusts ≥ 45 mph (gusts ≥ 72 km/h)).
+- Observed heat uses one national threshold (feels-like ≥ 104 °F (feels-like ≥ 40 °C)); FEMA heat waves follow local heat-alert criteria, so the two can differ.
+**Q: What is the weather risk at our Boise hub?**
+> Boise is not one of the hubs in our weather-risk coverage, so I can’t assess its risk. I can help assess any of our listed hubs.
+- **Out of scope:** yes, politely declined, no tools called
+- Boise is not included in the covered hub data.

input.content:
# Design How Sneakoscope is built, and why. This page is written for someone who has never seen the code. Every part links to the folder, file or line that does the work. Every choice is explained in plain words here, and the full reasoning behind each one is in the [decision log](decisions.md) (D-numbers like **D56** point there). ## Contents 1. [The big picture](#1-the-big-picture) 2. [Architecture: the parts and how they talk](#2-architecture-the-parts-and-how-they-talk) 3. [How the LLM is kept from inventing numbers](#3-how-the-llm-is-kept-from-inventing-numbers) 4. [One question, end to end](#4-one-question-end-to-end) 5. [How a hub's risk score is computed](#5-how-a-hubs-risk-score-is-computed) 6. [Where the data comes from: ingest and the nightly job](#6-where-the-data-comes-from-ingest-and-the-nightly-job) 7. [Data storage: tables, and why Postgres](#7-data-storage-tables-and-why-postgres) 8. [Repository structure](#8-repository-structure) 9. [Errors, security and limits](#9-errors-security-and-limits) 10. [Evals, and how the model was chosen](#10-evals-and-how-the-model-was-chosen) 11. [Ten decisions that shaped it](#11-ten-decisions-that-shaped-it) 12. [Trade-offs, and what I'd do next](#12-trade-offs-and-what-id-do-next) --- ## 1. The big picture Analysts at a logistics company ask, in plain English, which of the company's **36 US distribution hubs** are most exposed to severe weather. For example: *"Which Midwest hubs are most exposed to winter disruption?"* or *"Why is Dallas high risk?"*. The answers help them decide where to invest in resilience upgrades. **The one rule everything is built around:** *the LLM never produces a number.* Every score, rank, count and percentage is calculated by plain, tested TypeScript. The LLM only decides **which tool to call** and **explains what the tool returned**. Then code checks the explanation before anyone sees it. ## 2. Architecture: the parts and how they talk ```mermaid flowchart TB user([Analyst in a browser]) subgraph vercel [Vercel: one Next.js app] ui["Chat UI
src/app/_components"] proxy["Login check
src/proxy.ts"] api["API routes
src/app/api"] subgraph core ["src/core: plain TypeScript, no Next.js"] agent["Agent
agent/"] tools["4 tools
agent/tools/"] scoring["Scoring and stats
scoring/, stats/"] ingest["Ingest pipeline
ingest/, pipeline/"] repos["Database access
db/"] end end cron([Vercel Cron, daily 06:00 UTC]) db[(Supabase Postgres)] llm[OpenRouter: gpt-6.1-terra] meteo[Open-Meteo weather archive] fema[FEMA National Risk Index] user --> proxy --> ui ui -- "POST /api/chat, GET /api/widgets, …" --> api api --> agent agent <-- "chooses tools, writes the answer" --> llm agent --> tools --> scoring tools --> repos cron -- "GET /api/cron/ingest" --> api api --> ingest ingest --> meteo ingest --> fema ingest --> repos repos --> db ``` | Part | Where | What it does | Talks to | |---|---|---|---| | **Chat UI** | [src/app/_components/](../src/app/_components/) | The page: chat, the list of earlier chats, the overview widgets. Entry: [`SneakoscopeApp`](../src/app/_components/SneakoscopeApp.tsx#L55) | Only our own API routes, never the LLM | | **Login check** | [src/proxy.ts](../src/proxy.ts) | Asks for the site username/password on every page and API ([`proxy`](../src/proxy.ts#L18)) | — | | **API routes** | [src/app/api/](../src/app/api/) | Thin: check the login, validate the request with Zod, call `src/core`, turn errors into friendly JSON | `src/core` | | **Agent** | [src/core/agent/](../src/core/agent/) | Runs the LLM with tools, checks the answer, retries once | OpenRouter, the tools | | **Tools** | [src/core/agent/tools/](../src/core/agent/tools/) | `rank_hubs`, `compare_hubs`, `get_weather_stat`, `explain_hub_score`. They compute; the LLM only calls them | Scoring, stats, database | | **Scoring and stats** | [src/core/scoring/](../src/core/scoring/), [src/core/stats/](../src/core/stats/) | Pure functions: weather days → hazard scores → overall score, level, confidence | Nothing (pure) | | **Ingest pipeline** | [src/core/ingest/](../src/core/ingest/), [src/core/pipeline/](../src/core/pipeline/) | Fetches new weather + FEMA data, then re-scores every hub | Open-Meteo, FEMA, database | | **Database access** | [src/core/db/](../src/core/db/) | One small "repository" file per table | Supabase | **Why `src/core` has no Next.js in it:** the agent and scoring can then run and be tested on their own: from unit tests, from `npm run ask` in a terminal, and from the evals. An ESLint rule in [eslint.config.mjs](../eslint.config.mjs) fails the build if anything in `src/core` imports Next.js or React (D31). ## 3. How the LLM is kept from inventing numbers Five layers, each in code: 1. **Tools do all the math.** The LLM can't compute a score. It has to call a tool, and the tool returns finished numbers from tested functions. Even differences between hubs are computed for it: `rank_hubs` returns a `spread`, and `compare_hubs` returns `gaps` ([`scoreSpread`](../src/core/scoring/ranking.ts#L89), D98). 2. **Every input and output has a strict shape (Zod).** Each tool's input is a Zod schema, and so is the final answer the LLM must return: [`llmAnswerSchema`](../src/core/agent/answerSchema.ts#L28). It has the answer text, hubs mentioned, the numbers used, the premise claim, confidence, assumptions, limitations, follow-ups, an optional recommendation, and the out-of-scope flag. An answer that doesn't fit the shape is rejected. 3. **A ledger records every tool result.** [`ToolLedger`](../src/core/agent/ledger.ts#L114) is the ground truth for one answer: which hubs and numbers the tools actually returned. In a follow-up it also includes the earlier turns' results (D65). 4. **Code checks the answer against the ledger:** [`finalizeAnswer`](../src/core/agent/finalizeAnswer.ts#L40). - *Hard checks* (on failure, the LLM gets one retry with the list of problems): every hub mentioned and every number in `dataUsed` must appear in the ledger. A recommendation needs data. A premise must be about a real hub. - *Soft check* (a warning, logged and counted by the evals): numbers in the free text that no tool returned. - If the retry also fails, the user gets a clear, friendly error, never an unchecked answer ([`runAgent`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L146)). 5. **Code, not the LLM, sets the sensitive fields.** Confidence is recomputed from the data. The premise verdict ("you said Dallas is high; the data says…") is decided by comparing against the real level. The standing data caveats are attached. Every recommendation gets a fixed disclaimer the LLM can't soften ([`RECOMMENDATION_DISCLAIMER`](../src/core/agent/config.ts#L25)). The evals then test all of this from the outside (section 10). ## 4. One question, end to end ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as Browser (Chat UI) participant R as POST /api/chat participant Q as answerQuestion participant A as runAgent participant L as LLM (OpenRouter) participant T as Tools participant D as Database B->>R: { sessionId, message, units } R->>Q: login + Zod check passed Q->>D: load latest scores + this chat's history Q->>A: question, history, hub data loop up to 6 tool steps A->>L: system prompt + messages + tool list L->>T: call a tool (e.g. explain_hub_score) T-->>A: numbers (recorded in the ledger) A-->>B: progress: "Looking at Dallas…" end L-->>A: structured final answer (streamed) A-->>B: answer text as it is written A->>A: finalizeAnswer: check against the ledger (retry once if needed) Q->>D: save the turn + log events R-->>B: the validated answer (data-answer) ``` Step by step, with the code: 1. **The browser sends the question.** [`SneakoscopeApp`](../src/app/_components/SneakoscopeApp.tsx#L55) uses the AI SDK's `useChat` to `POST /api/chat` with `{ sessionId, message, units }`. The session id lives in the browser's localStorage, so earlier chats can be reopened from the side menu. 2. **The route checks and hands off.** [`POST`](../src/app/api/chat/route.ts#L20) checks the login again (the proxy is the first layer), validates the body with Zod ([`chatRequestSchema`](../src/core/api/chatStream.ts#L20)), and starts a stream ([`buildChatStream`](../src/core/api/chatStream.ts#L56)). 3. **Context and memory are loaded.** [`answerQuestion`](../src/core/agent/answerQuestion.ts#L54) loads the latest score for every hub ([`loadAgentContext`](../src/core/agent/context.ts#L58)) and the last 10 turns of this chat ([`loadHistory`](../src/core/db/chatRepository.ts#L52)). 4. **The agent runs.** [`runAgent`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L146) builds the system prompt ([`buildSystemPrompt`](../src/core/agent/systemPrompt.ts#L27): rules, the scoring method, the hub list) and the tools ([`buildTools`](../src/core/agent/tools/index.ts#L21)), then calls the LLM in [`attempt`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L70). Limits: 6 tool steps, 25 s per step, 60 s in total ([`AGENT_LIMITS`](../src/core/agent/config.ts#L8)). 5. **Tools compute.** Every tool call goes through [`runTool`](../src/core/agent/tools/shared.ts#L44). It reports progress to the browser, records the result in the ledger, and answers an exact repeat of an earlier call with a short "same as before" note instead of re-running it (D96). 6. **The answer streams.** The LLM's answer text streams to the browser as it's written, so the analyst sees it appear. 7. **Code checks it.** [`finalizeAnswer`](../src/core/agent/finalizeAnswer.ts#L40) runs the checks from section 3. If they fail, the browser shows "Double-checking my numbers…" while the LLM gets one retry. 8. **Saved and logged.** The turn, including tool results, is saved for follow-ups ([`saveTurn`](../src/core/db/chatRepository.ts#L94)), and an `agent.answered` event is logged with the tools used, tokens and confidence ([`recordEvent`](../src/core/db/eventsRepository.ts#L50)). 9. **The browser shows the checked answer.** Visuals (score breakdown, comparison grid, monthly pattern) are drawn **from the tool results**, not from anything the LLM wrote ([src/app/_components/visuals/](../src/app/_components/visuals/)). ## 5. How a hub's risk score is computed All numbers live in one file, [src/core/scoring/config.ts](../src/core/scoring/config.ts). The method: - **Six hazards, weighted** ([`HAZARD_WEIGHTS`](../src/core/scoring/config.ts#L68)): hurricane 25%, winter 20%, flood/heavy rain 20%, severe storms (tornado + hail) 15%, wind 10%, heat 10%. - **Each hazard is scored 0–100 on a fixed national scale**, so a score means the same thing for every hub. Most hazards blend two sources 50/50: - **Observed weather:** days over a threshold in the last 5 years, from Open-Meteo. Example: snow days ≥ 1 cm. - **FEMA's long-term frequency** for the hub's county. Hurricane and severe storms use FEMA only ([`computeHazardScores`](../src/core/scoring/hazards.ts#L106)). - **Overall = 0.6 × weighted average + 0.4 × worst hazard** ([`computeOverall`](../src/core/scoring/overall.ts#L24)). This way one severe hazard isn't averaged away: a hurricane hub isn't "medium" just because it never snows. - **Levels:** Low 0–33, Medium 34–66, High 67–100 ([`riskLevelFor`](../src/core/scoring/overall.ts#L38)). - **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed, not guessed ([`hybridConfidence`](../src/core/scoring/confidence.ts#L27)). It drops when data is missing, or when the two sources **disagree** by more than 40 points. The check compares like with like (D56). - **Putting it together:** [`scoreHub`](../src/core/scoring/scoreHub.ts#L23) returns a full, explainable breakdown, so the agent can say exactly where every point came from. What the score does and doesn't mean (it measures exposure, not losses) is spelled out in [assumptions.md](assumptions.md). ## 6. Where the data comes from: ingest and the nightly job ``` Vercel Cron 06:00 UTC ─► GET /api/cron/ingest ─► runIngestThenScore ├─ runIngest: per hub, fetch only the missing days │ (+ re-fetch the last 7, which the source revises) └─ runScoring: re-score all 36 hubs → new score snapshot ``` - **Ingest** ([`runIngest`](../src/core/ingest/runIngest.ts#L131)) is **incremental**. For each hub it works out which days are missing ([`planWeatherRange`](../src/core/ingest/planWeatherRange.ts#L34)), fetches them from Open-Meteo ([`fetchDailyWeather`](../src/core/data/openMeteo.ts#L132)), and stores them. FEMA data is fetched once per hub ([`fetchFemaCountyByPoint`](../src/core/data/femaNri.ts#L124)). A rate limiter keeps us under 90% of Open-Meteo's free limits ([`WeightedRateLimiter`](../src/core/ingest/rateLimiter.ts#L62)). A hub that failed to ingest is still scored on the data it already has. - **The nightly job** ([`GET`](../src/app/api/cron/ingest/route.ts#L21)) runs both ([`runIngestThenScore`](../src/core/pipeline/runIngestThenScore.ts#L23)). It's scheduled in [vercel.json](../vercel.json) and protected by a secret only Vercel sends (`CRON_SECRET`). - Every step logs an event (`ingest.started`, `ingest.weather_saved`, `scoring.finished`, …), so a failed night can be traced afterwards. ## 7. Data storage: tables, and why Postgres **Supabase Postgres** (hosted, free tier), created by the SQL files in [supabase/migrations/](../supabase/migrations/). | Table | What it holds | Size today | |---|---|---| | `hubs` | The 36 hubs: id (e.g. `kansas-city`), name, state, Census region, coordinates, time zone, county | 36 rows | | `weather_daily` | One row per hub per day: snowfall, min temperature, rain, max wind gust, max "feels-like" temperature | 77,544 rows (2021-01-01 → yesterday) | | `fema_nri` | Per hub: FEMA's yearly frequency for each hazard + the raw record | 36 rows | | `score_snapshots` | Per hub per scoring run: overall, level, top hazard, full breakdown, confidence, data window, scoring version | 36 per run | | `chat_sessions`, `chat_messages` | Conversation memory, including tool results, so follow-ups work | grows with use | | `events` | Append-only log: ingest runs, scoring, answers, retries, failures, eval runs; grouped by `correlation_id` | grows with use | Every table has `created_at` and `updated_at` (kept current by a trigger), and **row-level security is on with no public policies**. Only the server, holding the secret key, can read or write ([`getDb`](../src/core/db/client.ts#L24)). The browser never talks to the database. **Why Postgres (and why Supabase):** - The data is **small and relational**: hubs → days → scores. 77k rows is tiny for Postgres. - **One store for everything**: weather cache, FEMA data, score history, chat memory and the event log. No extra services to run or pay for. - **SQL makes checking easy.** The evals compute their expected answers from the same data, and ad-hoc questions ("how many snow days did Denver have?") are one query. - **Hosted, free, and close to Vercel** (both in the US East region). Hubs are rows, not code, so adding a city means adding a row. - *Not chosen:* a JSON file or SQLite (no persistence on Vercel's serverless functions), or a vector database (nothing here needs semantic search). ## 8. Repository structure ``` src/ app/ Next.js only: pages, API routes, React components _components/ the chat UI (answer cards in answer/, charts in visuals/) api/ chat, chat/history, chat/sessions, widgets, cron/ingest proxy.ts site login (HTTP Basic Auth) for every page and API core/ plain TypeScript, no Next.js (ESLint-enforced), all the logic: agent/ the agent: prompt, answer schema, ledger, checks, retry, the 4 tools api/ chat-stream protocol shared by the route and the UI config/ env variable validation, timeouts, ingest settings data/ clients for Open-Meteo and FEMA (with timeouts and retries) db/ one repository per table (Supabase) domain/ core types (Hub) errors/ BoundaryError (log format) and the friendly user errors ingest/, pipeline/ incremental ingest, rate limiting, ingest → score judge/ the independent answer judge used by the evals scoring/ hazard scores, overall, levels, confidence, caveats (pure) security/ login and cron-secret checks (constant-time) stats/, utils/ weather statistics, dates, units (pure) widgets/ data for the overview panel scripts/ CLI entry points: ingest, score, ask, eval, bakeoff, session:export, … evals/ the 13 eval cases, the oracle, the judge runner, reports supabase/migrations/ the database schema and the 36-hub seed docs/ this design, decisions, assumptions, plan, evals, bakeoff, examples, session log ``` ## 9. Errors, security and limits - **One log format for every failure at a boundary** (external API, database, LLM, API route, config): `ErrorName || message || function || emoji`, with a fixed emoji per boundary: 🦉 LLM, 🐸 Open-Meteo, 🦡 FEMA, 🐘 database, 🦄 API route, 🦔 config ([`BoundaryError`](../src/core/errors/boundaryError.ts#L56), [`BOUNDARY_EMOJI`](../src/core/errors/boundaryError.ts#L15)). A log line shows at a glance where something broke. - **Users never see raw errors.** [`toUserError`](../src/core/errors/userErrors.ts#L82) turns any failure into `{ code, message, hint, retryable }` with friendly copy, e.g. *"I couldn't put together an answer I can stand behind this time."* - **Every external call has a timeout:** HTTP 30 s, database 15 s, each LLM step 25 s ([src/core/config/timeouts.ts](../src/core/config/timeouts.ts)). - **Login:** HTTP Basic Auth on every page and API, checked in the proxy and again in each route, with constant-time comparison ([`isSiteAuthorized`](../src/core/security/auth.ts#L56)). The cron route uses its own secret instead ([`isCronAuthorized`](../src/core/security/auth.ts#L71)). - **Secrets** live only in `.env.local` (local, git-ignored) and Vercel's environment variables. Every variable is validated with Zod at startup, and errors name the missing variable, never its value ([src/core/config/env.ts](../src/core/config/env.ts)). [.env.example](../.env.example) lists them all, and a test fails if the two drift apart. ## 10. Evals, and how the model was chosen - **`npm run eval`** runs 13 cases: the brief's four questions, plus a false premise, a follow-up, an unknown city, a hazard we don't score, a decision question, an off-topic request, "last year", confidence and the top 5 ([`EVAL_CASES`](../evals/cases.ts#L22)). - The **expected values are computed at run time** from the same data the agent sees ([`buildOracle`](../evals/lib/oracle.ts#L38)), so they stay correct after every nightly re-score. - The checks are concrete: the right tool with the right input, the right top hub, numbers that match, the premise verdict. - **An independent judge** (an LLM from a different provider, `google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite`) grades each answer against the exact tool results ([`judgeAnswer`](../src/core/judge/judgeAnswer.ts#L122)). It's tested before every run with planted good and bad answers ([`judgeSelfTest`](../evals/lib/judging.ts#L96)). - **The model was picked by measurement.** 9 models were screened, then 4 finalists ran 3 times each, with the rule *never wrong on data → most accurate → cheapest → fastest*. `openai/gpt-6.1-terra` won: 39/39, about $0.01 per answer ([bakeoff.md](bakeoff.md)). The latest results are in [evals.md](evals.md), and real answers in [examples.md](examples.md). ## 11. Ten decisions that shaped it | # | Decision | Why | |---|---|---| | [D2](decisions.md) | The LLM never produces numbers; tools compute, code checks | Wrong numbers are the worst failure for a decision-support tool | | [D31](decisions.md) | `src/core` has no Next.js, enforced by lint | The logic can be tested and run from scripts and evals | | [D51](decisions.md), [D56](decisions.md) | Confidence is computed from completeness and whether sources agree, like with like | Honest uncertainty, not a guess | | [D53](decisions.md) | Tornadoes scored per 1,000 sq mi | FEMA's county data otherwise rewards big counties | | [D58](decisions.md) | Overall = 0.6 × average + 0.4 × worst hazard | One severe hazard shouldn't be averaged away | | [D65](decisions.md) | Follow-ups may reuse earlier tool results | Real conversations; no re-fetching the same data | | G5 in [D-table](decisions.md) | Code decides whether a question's premise is true | "Why is Seattle's hurricane risk high?" gets a correction, not an excuse | | [D96](decisions.md), [D98](decisions.md) | Duplicate tool calls answered in code; differences computed by tools | Fewer wasted steps, no model arithmetic | | [D103](decisions.md) | The judge's faithfulness score is the only judge-based hard check | Its pass/fail verdict flipped on identical answers | | [D110](decisions.md) | gpt-6.1-terra, chosen by a 9-model bakeoff | Most accurate and about 6× cheaper than the starting model | ## 12. Trade-offs, and what I'd do next **Trade-offs made on purpose:** - **Exposure, not losses.** Without shipment volumes or building data, the score answers "how often does bad weather hit here", not "where do we lose the most money". The agent says so. - **City-center points.** Each hub is its metro's center. Real warehouses may sit 20 km away, in another county. - **Historical only.** No forecasts or live alerts in this version. - **Free data sources.** Open-Meteo's free tier is non-commercial, so production would need their paid plan. **Next, in order** (also in [plan.md](plan.md)): 1. **Scoring v2:** score inland flood per county area, like tornadoes. The FEMA flood half is at 100 for most big metros today (D97). 2. **Live "Reviewed" badge:** run the judge in the background after each answer is shown (D99). 3. **Dust storms** from NOAA's Storm Events database: the brief mentions them, and the agent currently says they aren't scored. 4. **Forecasts and active NWS alerts**, hub volume weighting, and per-hub local thresholds (the same 5 cm of snow means more in Atlanta than in Minneapolis).

# Design How Sneakoscope is built, and why. This page is written for someone who has never seen the code. Every part links to the folder, file or line that does the work. Every choice is explained in plain words here, and the full reasoning behind each one is in the [decision log](decisions.md) (D-numbers like **D56** point there). ## Contents 1. [The big picture](#1-the-big-picture) 2. [Architecture: the parts and how they talk](#2-architecture-the-parts-and-how-they-talk) 3. [How the LLM is kept from inventing numbers](#3-how-the-llm-is-kept-from-inventing-numbers) 4. [One question, end to end](#4-one-question-end-to-end) 5. [How a hub's risk score is computed](#5-how-a-hubs-risk-score-is-computed) 6. [Where the data comes from: ingest and the nightly job](#6-where-the-data-comes-from-ingest-and-the-nightly-job) 7. [Data storage: tables, and why Postgres](#7-data-storage-tables-and-why-postgres) 8. [Repository structure](#8-repository-structure) 9. [Errors, security and limits](#9-errors-security-and-limits) 10. [Evals, and how the model was chosen](#10-evals-and-how-the-model-was-chosen) 11. [Ten decisions that shaped it](#11-ten-decisions-that-shaped-it) 12. [Trade-offs, and what I'd do next](#12-trade-offs-and-what-id-do-next) --- ## 1. The big picture Analysts at a logistics company ask, in plain English, which of the company's **36 US distribution hubs** are most exposed to severe weather. For example: *"Which Midwest hubs are most exposed to winter disruption?"* or *"Why is Dallas high risk?"*. The answers help them decide where to invest in resilience upgrades. **The one rule everything is built around:** *the LLM never produces a number.* Every score, rank, count and percentage is calculated by plain, tested TypeScript. The LLM only decides **which tool to call** and **explains what the tool returned**. Then code checks the explanation before anyone sees it. ## 2. Architecture: the parts and how they talk ```mermaid flowchart TB user([Analyst in a browser]) subgraph vercel [Vercel: one Next.js app] ui["Chat UI
src/app/_components"] proxy["Login check
src/proxy.ts"] api["API routes
src/app/api"] subgraph core ["src/core: plain TypeScript, no Next.js"] agent["Agent
agent/"] tools["4 tools
agent/tools/"] scoring["Scoring and stats
scoring/, stats/"] ingest["Ingest pipeline
ingest/, pipeline/"] repos["Database access
db/"] end end cron([Vercel Cron, daily 06:00 UTC]) db[(Supabase Postgres)] llm[OpenRouter: gpt-6.1-terra] meteo[Open-Meteo weather archive] fema[FEMA National Risk Index] user --> proxy --> ui ui -- "POST /api/chat, GET /api/widgets, …" --> api api --> agent agent <-- "chooses tools, writes the answer" --> llm agent --> tools --> scoring tools --> repos cron -- "GET /api/cron/ingest" --> api api --> ingest ingest --> meteo ingest --> fema ingest --> repos repos --> db ``` | Part | Where | What it does | Talks to | |---|---|---|---| | **Chat UI** | [src/app/_components/](../src/app/_components/) | The page: chat, the list of earlier chats, the overview widgets. Entry: [`SneakoscopeApp`](../src/app/_components/SneakoscopeApp.tsx#L55) | Only our own API routes, never the LLM | | **Login check** | [src/proxy.ts](../src/proxy.ts) | Asks for the site username/password on every page and API ([`proxy`](../src/proxy.ts#L18)) | — | | **API routes** | [src/app/api/](../src/app/api/) | Thin: check the login, validate the request with Zod, call `src/core`, turn errors into friendly JSON | `src/core` | | **Agent** | [src/core/agent/](../src/core/agent/) | Runs the LLM with tools, checks the answer, retries once | OpenRouter, the tools | | **Tools** | [src/core/agent/tools/](../src/core/agent/tools/) | `rank_hubs`, `compare_hubs`, `get_weather_stat`, `explain_hub_score`. They compute; the LLM only calls them | Scoring, stats, database | | **Scoring and stats** | [src/core/scoring/](../src/core/scoring/), [src/core/stats/](../src/core/stats/) | Pure functions: weather days → hazard scores → overall score, level, confidence | Nothing (pure) | | **Ingest pipeline** | [src/core/ingest/](../src/core/ingest/), [src/core/pipeline/](../src/core/pipeline/) | Fetches new weather + FEMA data, then re-scores every hub | Open-Meteo, FEMA, database | | **Database access** | [src/core/db/](../src/core/db/) | One small "repository" file per table | Supabase | **Why `src/core` has no Next.js in it:** the agent and scoring can then run and be tested on their own: from unit tests, from `npm run ask` in a terminal, and from the evals. An ESLint rule in [eslint.config.mjs](../eslint.config.mjs) fails the build if anything in `src/core` imports Next.js or React (D31). ## 3. How the LLM is kept from inventing numbers Five layers, each in code: 1. **Tools do all the math.** The LLM can't compute a score. It has to call a tool, and the tool returns finished numbers from tested functions. Even differences between hubs are computed for it: `rank_hubs` returns a `spread`, and `compare_hubs` returns `gaps` ([`scoreSpread`](../src/core/scoring/ranking.ts#L89), D98). 2. **Every input and output has a strict shape (Zod).** Each tool's input is a Zod schema, and so is the final answer the LLM must return: [`llmAnswerSchema`](../src/core/agent/answerSchema.ts#L28). It has the answer text, hubs mentioned, the numbers used, the premise claim, confidence, assumptions, limitations, follow-ups, an optional recommendation, and the out-of-scope flag. An answer that doesn't fit the shape is rejected. 3. **A ledger records every tool result.** [`ToolLedger`](../src/core/agent/ledger.ts#L114) is the ground truth for one answer: which hubs and numbers the tools actually returned. In a follow-up it also includes the earlier turns' results (D65). 4. **Code checks the answer against the ledger:** [`finalizeAnswer`](../src/core/agent/finalizeAnswer.ts#L40). - *Hard checks* (on failure, the LLM gets one retry with the list of problems): every hub mentioned and every number in `dataUsed` must appear in the ledger. A recommendation needs data. A premise must be about a real hub. - *Soft check* (a warning, logged and counted by the evals): numbers in the free text that no tool returned. - If the retry also fails, the user gets a clear, friendly error, never an unchecked answer ([`runAgent`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L146)). 5. **Code, not the LLM, sets the sensitive fields.** Confidence is recomputed from the data. The premise verdict ("you said Dallas is high; the data says…") is decided by comparing against the real level. The standing data caveats are attached. Every recommendation gets a fixed disclaimer the LLM can't soften ([`RECOMMENDATION_DISCLAIMER`](../src/core/agent/config.ts#L25)). The session id lives in the browser's localStorage, so earlier chats can be reopened from the side menu. 2. **The route checks and hands off.** [`POST`](../src/app/api/chat/route.ts#L20) checks the login again (the proxy is the first layer), validates the body with Zod ([`chatRequestSchema`](../src/core/api/chatStream.ts#L20)), and starts a stream ([`buildChatStream`](../src/core/api/chatStream.ts#L56)). 3. **Context and memory are loaded.** [`answerQuestion`](../src/core/agent/answerQuestion.ts#L54) loads the latest score for every hub ([`loadAgentContext`](../src/core/agent/context.ts#L58)) and the last 10 turns of this chat ([`loadHistory`](../src/core/db/chatRepository.ts#L52)). 4. **The agent runs.** [`runAgent`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L146) builds the system prompt ([`buildSystemPrompt`](../src/core/agent/systemPrompt.ts#L27): rules, the scoring method, the hub list) and the tools ([`buildTools`](../src/core/agent/tools/index.ts#L21)), then calls the LLM in [`attempt`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L70). Limits: 6 tool steps, 25 s per step, 60 s in total ([`AGENT_LIMITS`](../src/core/agent/config.ts#L8)). 5. **Tools compute.** Every tool call goes through [`runTool`](../src/core/agent/tools/shared.ts#L44). It reports progress to the browser, records the result in the ledger, and answers an exact repeat of an earlier call with a short "same as before" note instead of re-running it (D96). 6. **The answer streams.** The LLM's answer text streams to the browser as it's written, so the analyst sees it appear. 7. **Code checks it.** [`finalizeAnswer`](../src/core/agent/finalizeAnswer.ts#L40) runs the checks from section 3. How a hub's risk score is computed All numbers live in one file, [src/core/scoring/config.ts](../src/core/scoring/config.ts). The method: - **Six hazards, weighted** ([`HAZARD_WEIGHTS`](../src/core/scoring/config.ts#L68)): hurricane 25%, winter 20%, flood/heavy rain 20%, severe storms (tornado + hail) 15%, wind 10%, heat 10%. - **Each hazard is scored 0–100 on a fixed national scale**, so a score means the same thing for every hub. Most hazards blend two sources 50/50: - **Observed weather:** days over a threshold in the last 5 years, from Open-Meteo. # Design How Sneakoscope is built, and why. This page is written for someone who has never seen the code. Every part links to the folder, file or line that does the work. Every choice is explained in plain words here, and the full reasoning behind each one is in the [decision log](decisions.md) (D-numbers like **D56** point there). ## Contents 1. [The big picture](#1-the-big-picture) 2. [Architecture: the parts and how they talk](#2-architecture-the-parts-and-how-they-talk) 3. [How the LLM is kept from inventing numbers](#3-how-the-llm-is-kept-from-inventing-numbers) 4. [One question, end to end](#4-one-question-end-to-end) 5. [How a hub's risk score is computed](#5-how-a-hubs-risk-score-is-computed) 6. [Where the data comes from: ingest and the nightly job](#6-where-the-data-comes-from-ingest-and-the-nightly-job) 7. [Data storage: tables, and why Postgres](#7-data-storage-tables-and-why-postgres) 8. [Repository structure](#8-repository-structure) 9. [Errors, security and limits](#9-errors-security-and-limits) 10. [Evals, and how the model was chosen](#10-evals-and-how-the-model-was-chosen) 11. [Ten decisions that shaped it](#11-ten-decisions-that-shaped-it) 12. [Trade-offs, and what I'd do next](#12-trade-offs-and-what-id-do-next) --- ## 1. The big picture Analysts at a logistics company ask, in plain English, which of the company's **36 US distribution hubs** are most exposed to severe weather. For example: *"Which Midwest hubs are most exposed to winter disruption?"* or *"Why is Dallas high risk?"*. The answers help them decide where to invest in resilience upgrades. **The one rule everything is built around:** *the LLM never produces a number.* Every score, rank, count and percentage is calculated by plain, tested TypeScript. The LLM only decides **which tool to call** and **explains what the tool returned**. Then code checks the explanation before anyone sees it. ## 2. Architecture: the parts and how they talk ```mermaid flowchart TB user([Analyst in a browser]) subgraph vercel [Vercel: one Next.js app] ui["Chat UI
src/app/_components"] proxy["Login check
src/proxy.ts"] api["API routes
src/app/api"] subgraph core ["src/core: plain TypeScript, no Next.js"] agent["Agent
agent/"] tools["4 tools
agent/tools/"] scoring["Scoring and stats
scoring/, stats/"] ingest["Ingest pipeline
ingest/, pipeline/"] repos["Database access
db/"] end end cron([Vercel Cron, daily 06:00 UTC]) db[(Supabase Postgres)] llm[OpenRouter: gpt-6.1-terra] meteo[Open-Meteo weather archive] fema[FEMA National Risk Index] user --> proxy --> ui ui -- "POST /api/chat, GET /api/widgets, …" --> api api --> agent agent <-- "chooses tools, writes the answer" --> llm agent --> tools --> scoring tools --> repos cron -- "GET /api/cron/ingest" --> api api --> ingest ingest --> meteo ingest --> fema ingest --> repos repos --> db ``` | Part | Where | What it does | Talks to | |---|---|---|---| | **Chat UI** | [src/app/_components/](../src/app/_components/) | The page: chat, the list of earlier chats, the overview widgets. Entry: [`SneakoscopeApp`](../src/app/_components/SneakoscopeApp.tsx#L55) | Only our own API routes, never the LLM | | **Login check** | [src/proxy.ts](../src/proxy.ts) | Asks for the site username/password on every page and API ([`proxy`](../src/proxy.ts#L18)) | — | | **API routes** | [src/app/api/](../src/app/api/) | Thin: check the login, validate the request with Zod, call `src/core`, turn errors into friendly JSON | `src/core` | | **Agent** | [src/core/agent/](../src/core/agent/) | Runs the LLM with tools, checks the answer, retries once | OpenRouter, the tools | | **Tools** | [src/core/agent/tools/](../src/core/agent/tools/) | `rank_hubs`, `compare_hubs`, `get_weather_stat`, `explain_hub_score`. They compute; the LLM only calls them | Scoring, stats, database | | **Scoring and stats** | [src/core/scoring/](../src/core/scoring/), [src/core/stats/](../src/core/stats/) | Pure functions: weather days → hazard scores → overall score, level, confidence | Nothing (pure) | | **Ingest pipeline** | [src/core/ingest/](../src/core/ingest/), [src/core/pipeline/](../src/core/pipeline/) | Fetches new weather + FEMA data, then re-scores every hub | Open-Meteo, FEMA, database | | **Database access** | [src/core/db/](../src/core/db/) | One small "repository" file per table | Supabase | **Why `src/core` has no Next.js in it:** the agent and scoring can then run and be tested on their own: from unit tests, from `npm run ask` in a terminal, and from the evals. An ESLint rule in [eslint.config.mjs](../eslint.config.mjs) fails the build if anything in `src/core` imports Next.js or React (D31). ## 3. How the LLM is kept from inventing numbers Five layers, each in code: 1. **Tools do all the math.** The LLM can't compute a score. It has to call a tool, and the tool returns finished numbers from tested functions. Even differences between hubs are computed for it: `rank_hubs` returns a `spread`, and `compare_hubs` returns `gaps` ([`scoreSpread`](../src/core/scoring/ranking.ts#L89), D98). 2. **Every input and output has a strict shape (Zod).** Each tool's input is a Zod schema, and so is the final answer the LLM must return: [`llmAnswerSchema`](../src/core/agent/answerSchema.ts#L28). It has the answer text, hubs mentioned, the numbers used, the premise claim, confidence, assumptions, limitations, follow-ups, an optional recommendation, and the out-of-scope flag. An answer that doesn't fit the shape is rejected. 3. **A ledger records every tool result.** [`ToolLedger`](../src/core/agent/ledger.ts#L114) is the ground truth for one answer: which hubs and numbers the tools actually returned. In a follow-up it also includes the earlier turns' results (D65). 4. **Code checks the answer against the ledger:** [`finalizeAnswer`](../src/core/agent/finalizeAnswer.ts#L40). - *Hard checks* (on failure, the LLM gets one retry with the list of problems): every hub mentioned and every number in `dataUsed` must appear in the ledger. A recommendation needs data. A premise must be about a real hub. - *Soft check* (a warning, logged and counted by the evals): numbers in the free text that no tool returned. - If the retry also fails, the user gets a clear, friendly error, never an unchecked answer ([`runAgent`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L146)). 5. **Code, not the LLM, sets the sensitive fields.** Confidence is recomputed from the data. The premise verdict ("you said Dallas is high; the data says…") is decided by comparing against the real level. The standing data caveats are attached. Every recommendation gets a fixed disclaimer the LLM can't soften ([`RECOMMENDATION_DISCLAIMER`](../src/core/agent/config.ts#L25)). The evals then test all of this from the outside (section 10). ## 4. One question, end to end ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as Browser (Chat UI) participant R as POST /api/chat participant Q as answerQuestion participant A as runAgent participant L as LLM (OpenRouter) participant T as Tools participant D as Database B->>R: { sessionId, message, units } R->>Q: login + Zod check passed Q->>D: load latest scores + this chat's history Q->>A: question, history, hub data loop up to 6 tool steps A->>L: system prompt + messages + tool list L->>T: call a tool (e.g. explain_hub_score) T-->>A: numbers (recorded in the ledger) A-->>B: progress: "Looking at Dallas…" end L-->>A: structured final answer (streamed) A-->>B: answer text as it is written A->>A: finalizeAnswer: check against the ledger (retry once if needed) Q->>D: save the turn + log events R-->>B: the validated answer (data-answer) ``` Step by step, with the code: 1. **The browser sends the question.** [`SneakoscopeApp`](../src/app/_components/SneakoscopeApp.tsx#L55) uses the AI SDK's `useChat` to `POST /api/chat` with `{ sessionId, message, units }`. The session id lives in the browser's localStorage, so earlier chats can be reopened from the side menu. 2. **The route checks and hands off.** [`POST`](../src/app/api/chat/route.ts#L20) checks the login again (the proxy is the first layer), validates the body with Zod ([`chatRequestSchema`](../src/core/api/chatStream.ts#L20)), and starts a stream ([`buildChatStream`](../src/core/api/chatStream.ts#L56)). 3. **Context and memory are loaded.** [`answerQuestion`](../src/core/agent/answerQuestion.ts#L54) loads the latest score for every hub ([`loadAgentContext`](../src/core/agent/context.ts#L58)) and the last 10 turns of this chat ([`loadHistory`](../src/core/db/chatRepository.ts#L52)). 4. **The agent runs.** [`runAgent`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L146) builds the system prompt ([`buildSystemPrompt`](../src/core/agent/systemPrompt.ts#L27): rules, the scoring method, the hub list) and the tools ([`buildTools`](../src/core/agent/tools/index.ts#L21)), then calls the LLM in [`attempt`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L70). Limits: 6 tool steps, 25 s per step, 60 s in total ([`AGENT_LIMITS`](../src/core/agent/config.ts#L8)). 5. **Tools compute.** Every tool call goes through [`runTool`](../src/core/agent/tools/shared.ts#L44). It reports progress to the browser, records the result in the ledger, and answers an exact repeat of an earlier call with a short "same as before" note instead of re-running it (D96). 6. **The answer streams.** The LLM's answer text streams to the browser as it's written, so the analyst sees it appear. 7. **Code checks it.** [`finalizeAnswer`](../src/core/agent/finalizeAnswer.ts#L40) runs the checks from section 3. If they fail, the browser shows "Double-checking my numbers…" while the LLM gets one retry. 8. **Saved and logged.** The turn, including tool results, is saved for follow-ups ([`saveTurn`](../src/core/db/chatRepository.ts#L94)), and an `agent.answered` event is logged with the tools used, tokens and confidence ([`recordEvent`](../src/core/db/eventsRepository.ts#L50)). 9. **The browser shows the checked answer.** Visuals (score breakdown, comparison grid, monthly pattern) are drawn **from the tool results**, not from anything the LLM wrote ([src/app/_components/visuals/](../src/app/_components/visuals/)). ## 5. How a hub's risk score is computed All numbers live in one file, [src/core/scoring/config.ts](../src/core/scoring/config.ts). The method: - **Six hazards, weighted** ([`HAZARD_WEIGHTS`](../src/core/scoring/config.ts#L68)): hurricane 25%, winter 20%, flood/heavy rain 20%, severe storms (tornado + hail) 15%, wind 10%, heat 10%. - **Each hazard is scored 0–100 on a fixed national scale**, so a score means the same thing for every hub. Most hazards blend two sources 50/50: - **Observed weather:** days over a threshold in the last 5 years, from Open-Meteo. Example: snow days ≥ 1 cm. - **FEMA's long-term frequency** for the hub's county. Hurricane and severe storms use FEMA only ([`computeHazardScores`](../src/core/scoring/hazards.ts#L106)). - **Overall = 0.6 × weighted average + 0.4 × worst hazard** ([`computeOverall`](../src/core/scoring/overall.ts#L24)). This way one severe hazard isn't averaged away: a hurricane hub isn't "medium" just because it never snows. - **Levels:** Low 0–33, Medium 34–66, High 67–100 ([`riskLevelFor`](../src/core/scoring/overall.ts#L38)). - **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed, not guessed ([`hybridConfidence`](../src/core/scoring/confidence.ts#L27)). It drops when data is missing, or when the two sources **disagree** by more than 40 points. The check compares like with like (D56). - **Putting it together:** [`scoreHub`](../src/core/scoring/scoreHub.ts#L23) returns a full, explainable breakdown, so the agent can say exactly where every point came from. What the score does and doesn't mean (it measures exposure, not losses) is spelled out in [assumptions.md](assumptions.md). ## 6. Where the data comes from: ingest and the nightly job ``` Vercel Cron 06:00 UTC ─► GET /api/cron/ingest ─► runIngestThenScore ├─ runIngest: per hub, fetch only the missing days │ (+ re-fetch the last 7, which the source revises) └─ runScoring: re-score all 36 hubs → new score snapshot ``` - **Ingest** ([`runIngest`](../src/core/ingest/runIngest.ts#L131)) is **incremental**. For each hub it works out which days are missing ([`planWeatherRange`](../src/core/ingest/planWeatherRange.ts#L34)), fetches them from Open-Meteo ([`fetchDailyWeather`](../src/core/data/openMeteo.ts#L132)), and stores them. FEMA data is fetched once per hub ([`fetchFemaCountyByPoint`](../src/core/data/femaNri.ts#L124)). A rate limiter keeps us under 90% of Open-Meteo's free limits ([`WeightedRateLimiter`](../src/core/ingest/rateLimiter.ts#L62)). That's why the first full load (5 years × 36 hubs) takes about an hour, while the nightly top-up takes seconds. - **Scoring** ([`runScoring`](../src/core/scoring/runScoring.ts#L65)) reads the stored data, scores every hub and saves a snapshot per hub. A hub that failed to ingest is still scored on the data it already has. - **The nightly job** ([`GET`](../src/app/api/cron/ingest/route.ts#L21)) runs both ([`runIngestThenScore`](../src/core/pipeline/runIngestThenScore.ts#L23)). It's scheduled in [vercel.json](../vercel.json) and protected by a secret only Vercel sends (`CRON_SECRET`). - Every step logs an event (`ingest.started`, `ingest.weather_saved`, `scoring.finished`, …), so a failed night can be traced afterwards. ## 7. Data storage: tables, and why Postgres **Supabase Postgres** (hosted, free tier), created by the SQL files in [supabase/migrations/](../supabase/migrations/). | Table | What it holds | Size today | |---|---|---| | `hubs` | The 36 hubs: id (e.g. `kansas-city`), name, state, Census region, coordinates, time zone, county | 36 rows | | `weather_daily` | One row per hub per day: snowfall, min temperature, rain, max wind gust, max "feels-like" temperature | 77,544 rows (2021-01-01 → yesterday) | | `fema_nri` | Per hub: FEMA's yearly frequency for each hazard + the raw record | 36 rows | | `score_snapshots` | Per hub per scoring run: overall, level, top hazard, full breakdown, confidence, data window, scoring version | 36 per run | | `chat_sessions`, `chat_messages` | Conversation memory, including tool results, so follow-ups work | grows with use | | `events` | Append-only log: ingest runs, scoring, answers, retries, failures, eval runs; grouped by `correlation_id` | grows with use | Every table has `created_at` and `updated_at` (kept current by a trigger), and **row-level security is on with no public policies**. Only the server, holding the secret key, can read or write ([`getDb`](../src/core/db/client.ts#L24)). The browser never talks to the database. **Why Postgres (and why Supabase):** - The data is **small and relational**: hubs → days → scores. 77k rows is tiny for Postgres. - **One store for everything**: weather cache, FEMA data, score history, chat memory and the event log. No extra services to run or pay for. - **SQL makes checking easy.** The evals compute their expected answers from the same data, and ad-hoc questions ("how many snow days did Denver have?") are one query. - **Hosted, free, and close to Vercel** (both in the US East region). Hubs are rows, not code, so adding a city means adding a row. - *Not chosen:* a JSON file or SQLite (no persistence on Vercel's serverless functions), or a vector database (nothing here needs semantic search). ## 8. Repository structure ``` src/ app/ Next.js only: pages, API routes, React components _components/ the chat UI (answer cards in answer/, charts in visuals/) api/ chat, chat/history, chat/sessions, widgets, cron/ingest proxy.ts site login (HTTP Basic Auth) for every page and API core/ plain TypeScript, no Next.js (ESLint-enforced), all the logic: agent/ the agent: prompt, answer schema, ledger, checks, retry, the 4 tools api/ chat-stream protocol shared by the route and the UI config/ env variable validation, timeouts, ingest settings data/ clients for Open-Meteo and FEMA (with timeouts and retries) db/ one repository per table (Supabase) domain/ core types (Hub) errors/ BoundaryError (log format) and the friendly user errors ingest/, pipeline/ incremental ingest, rate limiting, ingest → score judge/ the independent answer judge used by the evals scoring/ hazard scores, overall, levels, confidence, caveats (pure) security/ login and cron-secret checks (constant-time) stats/, utils/ weather statistics, dates, units (pure) widgets/ data for the overview panel scripts/ CLI entry points: ingest, score, ask, eval, bakeoff, session:export, … evals/ the 13 eval cases, the oracle, the judge runner, reports supabase/migrations/ the database schema and the 36-hub seed docs/ this design, decisions, assumptions, plan, evals, bakeoff, examples, session log ``` ## 9. Errors, security and limits - **One log format for every failure at a boundary** (external API, database, LLM, API route, config): `ErrorName || message || function || emoji`, with a fixed emoji per boundary: 🦉 LLM, 🐸 Open-Meteo, 🦡 FEMA, 🐘 database, 🦄 API route, 🦔 config ([`BoundaryError`](../src/core/errors/boundaryError.ts#L56), [`BOUNDARY_EMOJI`](../src/core/errors/boundaryError.ts#L15)). A log line shows at a glance where something broke. - **Users never see raw errors.** [`toUserError`](../src/core/errors/userErrors.ts#L82) turns any failure into `{ code, message, hint, retryable }` with friendly copy, e.g. *"I couldn't put together an answer I can stand behind this time."* - **Every external call has a timeout:** HTTP 30 s, database 15 s, each LLM step 25 s ([src/core/config/timeouts.ts](../src/core/config/timeouts.ts)). - **Login:** HTTP Basic Auth on every page and API, checked in the proxy and again in each route, with constant-time comparison ([`isSiteAuthorized`](../src/core/security/auth.ts#L56)). Every variable is validated with Zod at startup, and errors name the missing variable, never its value ([src/core/config/env.ts](../src/core/config/env.ts)). +| **Login check** | [src/proxy.ts](../src/proxy.ts) | Asks for the site username/password on every page and API ([`proxy`](../src/proxy.ts#L18)) | — |
+| **API routes** | [src/app/api/](../src/app/api/) | Thin: check the login, validate the request with Zod, call `src/core`, turn errors into friendly JSON | `src/core` |
+| **Agent** | [src/core/agent/](../src/core/agent/) | Runs the LLM with tools, checks the answer, retries once | OpenRouter, the tools |

+| **Tools** | [src/core/agent/tools/](../src/core/agent/tools/) | `rank_hubs`, `compare_hubs`, `get_weather_stat`, `explain_hub_score`. They compute; the LLM only calls them | Scoring, stats, database |

+**Why `src/core` has no Next.js in it:** the agent and scoring can then run and be tested on their own: from unit tests,
+from `npm run ask` in a terminal, and from the evals. An ESLint rule in [eslint.config.mjs](../eslint.config.mjs)
+fails the build if anything in `src/core` imports Next.js or React (D31).
+## 3. How the LLM is kept from inventing numbers
+1. **Tools do all the math.** The LLM can't compute a score. It has to call a tool, and the tool returns finished
+   numbers from tested functions. Even differences between hubs are computed for it: `rank_hubs` returns a `spread`,
+2. **Every input and output has a strict shape (Zod).** Each tool's input is a Zod schema, and so is the final answer
+   the LLM must return: [`llmAnswerSchema`](../src/core/agent/answerSchema.ts#L28). It has the answer text, hubs
+   mentioned, the numbers used, the premise claim, confidence, assumptions, limitations, follow-ups, an optional
+   recommendation, and the out-of-scope flag. An answer that doesn't fit the shape is rejected.
+3. **A ledger records every tool result.** [`ToolLedger`](../src/core/agent/ledger.ts#L114) is the ground truth for one
+   answer: which hubs and numbers the tools actually returned. In a follow-up it also includes the earlier turns' results
+4. **Code checks the answer against the ledger:** [`finalizeAnswer`](../src/core/agent/finalizeAnswer.ts#L40).
+   - *Hard checks* (on failure, the LLM gets one retry with the list of problems): every hub mentioned and every number
+     in `dataUsed` must appear in the ledger. A recommendation needs data. A premise must be about a real hub.
+   - *Soft check* (a warning, logged and counted by the evals): numbers in the free text that no tool returned.
+   - If the retry also fails, the user gets a clear, friendly error, never an unchecked answer
+5. **Code, not the LLM, sets the sensitive fields.** Confidence is recomputed from the data. The premise verdict
+   ("you said Dallas is high; the data says…") is decided by comparing against the real level. The standing data
+   caveats are attached. Every recommendation gets a fixed disclaimer the LLM can't soften
+The evals then test all of this from the outside (section 10).
+  Q->>D: load latest scores + this chat's history
+    A->>L: system prompt + messages + tool list
+  A-->>B: answer text as it is written
+  A->>A: finalizeAnswer: check against the ledger (retry once if needed)
+  Q->>D: save the turn + log events
+1. **The browser sends the question.** [`SneakoscopeApp`](../src/app/_components/SneakoscopeApp.tsx#L55) uses the AI SDK's
+   `useChat` to `POST /api/chat` with `{ sessionId, message, units }`. The session id lives in the browser's
+   localStorage, so earlier chats can be reopened from the side menu.
+2. **The route checks and hands off.** [`POST`](../src/app/api/chat/route.ts#L20) checks the login again (the proxy is
+   the first layer), validates the body with Zod ([`chatRequestSchema`](../src/core/api/chatStream.ts#L20)), and starts a
+3. **Context and memory are loaded.** [`answerQuestion`](../src/core/agent/answerQuestion.ts#L54) loads the latest score
+   for every hub ([`loadAgentContext`](../src/core/agent/context.ts#L58)) and the last 10 turns of this chat
+4. **The agent runs.** [`runAgent`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L146) builds the system prompt
+   ([`buildSystemPrompt`](../src/core/agent/systemPrompt.ts#L27): rules, the scoring method, the hub list) and the
+   tools ([`buildTools`](../src/core/agent/tools/index.ts#L21)), then calls the LLM in
+   [`attempt`](../src/core/agent/runAgent.ts#L70). Limits: 6 tool steps, 25 s per step, 60 s in total
+5. **Tools compute.** Every tool call goes through [`runTool`](../src/core/agent/tools/shared.ts#L44). It reports progress
+   to the browser, records the result in the ledger, and answers an exact repeat of an earlier call with a short "same as
+   before" note instead of re-running it (D96).
+6. **The answer streams.** The LLM's answer text streams to the browser as it's written, so the analyst sees it appear.
+7. **Code checks it.** [`finalizeAnswer`](../src/core/agent/finalizeAnswer.ts#L40) runs the checks from section 3. If
+   they fail, the browser shows "Double-checking my numbers…" while the LLM gets one retry.
+8. **Saved and logged.** The turn, including tool results, is saved for follow-ups
+   ([`saveTurn`](../src/core/db/chatRepository.ts#L94)), and an `agent.answered` event is logged with the tools used,
+9. **The browser shows the checked answer.** Visuals (score breakdown, comparison grid, monthly pattern) are drawn
+   **from the tool results**, not from anything the LLM wrote ([src/app/_components/visuals/](../src/app/_components/visuals/)).
+## 5. How a hub's risk score is computed
+All numbers live in one file, [src/core/scoring/config.ts](../src/core/scoring/config.ts). The method:
+  flood/heavy rain 20%, severe storms (tornado + hail) 15%, wind 10%, heat 10%.
+- **Each hazard is scored 0–100 on a fixed national scale**, so a score means the same thing for every hub. Most hazards
+  - **Observed weather:** days over a threshold in the last 5 years, from Open-Meteo. Example: snow days ≥ 1 cm.
+  - **FEMA's long-term frequency** for the hub's county.
+  Hurricane and severe storms use FEMA only ([`computeHazardScores`](../src/core/scoring/hazards.ts#L106)).
+  This way one severe hazard isn't averaged away: a hurricane hub isn't "medium" just because it never snows.
+- **Confidence** (High / Medium / Low) is computed, not guessed ([`hybridConfidence`](../src/core/scoring/confidence.ts#L27)).
+  It drops when data is missing, or when the two sources **disagree** by more than 40 points. The check compares like
+- **Putting it together:** [`scoreHub`](../src/core/scoring/scoreHub.ts#L23) returns a full, explainable breakdown, so
+  the agent can say exactly where every point came from.
+What the score does and doesn't mean (it measures exposure, not losses) is spelled out in [assumptions.md](assumptions.md).
+## 6. Where the data comes from: ingest and the nightly job
+                                                   ├─ runIngest:  per hub, fetch only the missing days
+                                                   │             (+ re-fetch the last 7, which the source revises)
+                                                   └─ runScoring: re-score all 36 hubs → new score snapshot
+- **Ingest** ([`runIngest`](../src/core/ingest/runIngest.ts#L131)) is **incremental**. For each hub it works out which
+  days are missing ([`planWeatherRange`](../src/core/ingest/planWeatherRange.ts#L34)), fetches them from Open-Meteo
+  ([`fetchDailyWeather`](../src/core/data/openMeteo.ts#L132)), and stores them. FEMA data is fetched once per hub
+  ([`fetchFemaCountyByPoint`](../src/core/data/femaNri.ts#L124)). A rate limiter keeps us under 90% of Open-Meteo's free
+  limits ([`WeightedRateLimiter`](../src/core/ingest/rateLimiter.ts#L62)). That's why the first full load (5 years ×
+  36 hubs) takes about an hour, while the nightly top-up takes seconds.
+- **Scoring** ([`runScoring`](../src/core/scoring/runScoring.ts#L65)) reads the stored data, scores every hub and saves a
+  snapshot per hub. A hub that failed to ingest is still scored on the data it already has.
+  and protected by a secret only Vercel sends (`CRON_SECRET`).
+- Every step logs an event (`ingest.started`, `ingest.weather_saved`, `scoring.finished`, …), so a failed night can be
+## 7. Data storage: tables, and why Postgres
+**Supabase Postgres** (hosted, free tier), created by the SQL files in [supabase/migrations/](../supabase/migrations/).
+| Table | What it holds | Size today |
-| Chat UI + widgets | `src/app/` (Next.js App Router) | Only our own API routes |
-| Auth proxy | `src/proxy.ts` | Guards pages + API (Basic Auth); cron uses `CRON_SECRET` |
+| `hubs` | The 36 hubs: id (e.g. `kansas-city`), name, state, Census region, coordinates, time zone, county | 36 rows |
+| `weather_daily` | One row per hub per day: snowfall, min temperature, rain, max wind gust, max "feels-like" temperature | 77,544 rows (2021-01-01 → yesterday) |
+| `fema_nri` | Per hub: FEMA's yearly frequency for each hazard + the raw record | 36 rows |
+| `score_snapshots` | Per hub per scoring run: overall, level, top hazard, full breakdown, confidence, data window, scoring version | 36 per run |
+| `chat_sessions`, `chat_messages` | Conversation memory, including tool results, so follow-ups work | grows with use |
+| `events` | Append-only log: ingest runs, scoring, answers, retries, failures, eval runs; grouped by `correlation_id` | grows with use |
+Every table has `created_at` and `updated_at` (kept current by a trigger), and **row-level security is on with no
+public policies**. Only the server, holding the secret key, can read or write ([`getDb`](../src/core/db/client.ts#L24)).
+The browser never talks to the database.
+- The data is **small and relational**: hubs → days → scores. 77k rows is tiny for Postgres.
+- **One store for everything**: weather cache, FEMA data, score history, chat memory and the event log. No extra
+  services to run or pay for.
+- **SQL makes checking easy.** The evals compute their expected answers from the same data, and ad-hoc questions ("how
+  many snow days did Denver have?") are one query.
+- **Hosted, free, and close to Vercel** (both in the US East region). Hubs are rows, not code, so adding a city means
+- *Not chosen:* a JSON file or SQLite (no persistence on Vercel's serverless functions), or a vector database (nothing

+- **One log format for every failure at a boundary** (external API, database, LLM, API route, config):
+  `ErrorName || message || function || emoji`, with a fixed emoji per boundary: 🦉 LLM, 🐸 Open-Meteo, 🦡 FEMA,
+  [`BOUNDARY_EMOJI`](../src/core/errors/boundaryError.ts#L15)). A log line shows at a glance where something broke.
+- **Users never see raw errors.** [`toUserError`](../src/core/errors/userErrors.ts#L82) turns any failure into
+  `{ code, message, hint, retryable }` with friendly copy, e.g. *"I couldn't put together an answer I can stand behind
+- **Every external call has a timeout:** HTTP 30 s, database 15 s, each LLM step 25 s
+- **Login:** HTTP Basic Auth on every page and API, checked in the proxy and again in each route, with constant-time
+  comparison ([`isSiteAuthorized`](../src/core/security/auth.ts#L56)). The cron route uses its own secret instead
+- **Secrets** live only in `.env.local` (local, git-ignored) and Vercel's environment variables. Every variable is
+  validated with Zod at startup, and errors name the missing variable, never its value
+  ([src/core/config/env.ts](../src/core/config/env.ts)). [.env.example](../.env.example) lists them all, and a test
+  fails if the two drift apart.
+## 10. Evals, and how the model was chosen
+- **`npm run eval`** runs 13 cases: the brief's four questions, plus a false premise, a follow-up, an unknown city, a
+  hazard we don't score, a decision question, an off-topic request, "last year", confidence and the top 5
+  - The **expected values are computed at run time** from the same data the agent sees
+    ([`buildOracle`](../evals/lib/oracle.ts#L38)), so they stay correct after every nightly re-score.
+  - The checks are concrete: the right tool with the right input, the right top hub, numbers that match, the premise
+- **An independent judge** (an LLM from a different provider, `google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite`) grades each answer
+  against the exact tool results ([`judgeAnswer`](../src/core/judge/judgeAnswer.ts#L122)). It's tested before every run
+  with planted good and bad answers ([`judgeSelfTest`](../evals/lib/judging.ts#L96)).
+- **The model was picked by measurement.** 9 models were screened, then 4 finalists ran 3 times each, with the rule
+  *never wrong on data → most accurate → cheapest → fastest*. `openai/gpt-6.1-terra` won: 39/39, about $0.01 per answer
+  ([bakeoff.md](bakeoff.md)). The latest results are in [evals.md](evals.md), and real answers in [examples.md](examples.md).
+| [D2](decisions.md) | The LLM never produces numbers; tools compute, code checks | Wrong numbers are the worst failure for a decision-support tool |
+| [D31](decisions.md) | `src/core` has no Next.js, enforced by lint | The logic can be tested and run from scripts and evals |
+| [D51](decisions.md), [D56](decisions.md) | Confidence is computed from completeness and whether sources agree, like with like | Honest uncertainty, not a guess |
+| [D53](decisions.md) | Tornadoes scored per 1,000 sq mi | FEMA's county data otherwise rewards big counties |
+| [D58](decisions.md) | Overall = 0.6 × average + 0.4 × worst hazard | One severe hazard shouldn't be averaged away |
+| [D65](decisions.md) | Follow-ups may reuse earlier tool results | Real conversations; no re-fetching the same data |
+| G5 in [D-table](decisions.md) | Code decides whether a question's premise is true | "Why is Seattle's hurricane risk high?" gets a correction, not an excuse |
+| [D96](decisions.md), [D98](decisions.md) | Duplicate tool calls answered in code; differences computed by tools | Fewer wasted steps, no model arithmetic |
+| [D103](decisions.md) | The judge's faithfulness score is the only judge-based hard check | Its pass/fail verdict flipped on identical answers |
+| [D110](decisions.md) | gpt-6.1-terra, chosen by a 9-model bakeoff | Most accurate and about 6× cheaper than the starting model |
+## 12. Trade-offs, and what I'd do next
+- **Exposure, not losses.** Without shipment volumes or building data, the score answers "how often does bad weather
+  hit here", not "where do we lose the most money". The agent says so.
+- **City-center points.** Each hub is its metro's center. Real warehouses may sit 20 km away, in another county.
+- **Historical only.** No forecasts or live alerts in this version.
+- **Free data sources.** Open-Meteo's free tier is non-commercial, so production would need their paid plan.
+1. **Scoring v2:** score inland flood per county area, like tornadoes. The FEMA flood half is at 100 for most big metros
+2. **Live "Reviewed" badge:** run the judge in the background after each answer is shown (D99).
+3. **Dust storms** from NOAA's Storm Events database: the brief mentions them, and the agent currently says they aren't
+4. **Forecasts and active NWS alerts**, hub volume weighting, and per-hub local thresholds (the same 5 cm of snow means
+   more in Atlanta than in Minneapolis).

# Design & architecture

> Draft. Filled in as each step lands, and finalized in Step 9.

## System architecture
See the diagram in [plan.md](plan.md#architecture-target). Components:

| Component | Where | Talks to |
|---|---|---|
| Chat UI + widgets | `src/app/` (Next.js App Router) | Only our own API routes |
| API routes | `src/app/api/` | `src/core` |
| Auth proxy | `src/proxy.ts` | Guards pages + API (Basic Auth); cron uses `CRON_SECRET` |
| Agent | `src/core/agent/` | OpenRouter (LLM), tools |
| Tools | `src/core/tools/` | Repositories + scoring/stats |
| Scoring & stats | `src/core/scoring/`, `src/core/stats/` | Nothing: pure functions |
| Ingest | `src/core/ingest/` | Open-Meteo, FEMA NRI, Supabase |
| Repositories | `src/core/db/` | Supabase Postgres |

## Repository structure
```
src/app/         Next.js only (pages, API routes, components)
src/core/        framework-free logic (lint-enforced): config, domain, errors, db, …
scripts/         CLI entry points (db:check, session:export; later ingest, eval)
supabase/        SQL migrations (schema + hub seed)
docs/            plan, decisions, assumptions, design, session log
```

## Data storage choice
**Supabase Postgres**, because:
- The data is relational and small (36 hubs × ~2,200 days ≈ 80k weather rows).
- SQL makes the evals' "expected values" and ad-hoc analysis easy.
- It's hosted and free, and pairs well with Vercel.
- Built-in RLS lets us lock the tables down completely (server-only access).
- One store holds the hubs, the cached weather and FEMA data, score history, chat memory and the event log.
  No extra services.
